# PUBLISHER’S PREFACE.

Before the discovery of anesthetics, Animal Magnetism had deservedly come to attract general public attention, and probably no other work did as much to popularize the system as this one by Deleuze in its earlier editions.

Through repeated editions, it had attained a large circulation in this country, and, with its help, a science was being established that promised not only to prove a great curative agency in sickness and disease, but to banish a great deal of pain and suffering from the human family.

Under the influence of Magnetism, important and lengthy surgical operations have been carried out without the patient having the slightest awareness of pain, and with no ill effects; but as our hospitals and the medical profession at large adopted the use of anesthetics, Magnetism ceased to be used in practice, except by a few. But because so many fatal accidents—to say nothing of the large number of shattered nervous systems—have resulted from this dangerous agency, the public is beginning to ask if there is no substitute, and hundreds now endure pain rather than accept a worse alternative.

Having from time to time received requests for this work, which has been out of print for many years, we re-

<summary>The publisher explains that Deleuze's work on Animal Magnetism was highly popular before anesthetics replaced it, but safety concerns regarding chemical anesthetics are now prompting a renewed interest in reprinting the book.</summary>
<keywords>Animal Magnetism, Deleuze, anesthetics, surgical operations, medical profession, public safety, reprinting</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the Publisher's Preface from page iii, detailing the acquisition of a rare copy of the text and the ethical motivations for its republication.</meta>

resolved, if we could find a copy, to offer a new edition to the public by republishing it. Through the kindness of our friend, Dr. George M. Bourne of California, we were finally able to obtain one from the private hands of John McGraith of San Francisco.

We take special pleasure in presenting this book to the public at this time, believing it will supply a great public need, that it merits general public approval, and that the benefits under its direction will be many.

We can especially recommend the moral tone of the author, as his only desire seems to have been that he might be a blessing to the human race by teaching them the art of relieving pain and suffering. If there are those who would make an evil use of their Magnetic powers, there can be no better way of counteracting it than to place such information in the hands of the people as will enable them to understand its power and influence themselves, and in this way prevent and restrain any improper use of the principle.

NEW YORK, March, 1879.

# TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.

Since the first edition of this work was printed, the practice of <term>Mesmerism</term> has been greatly expanded, and it can be observed that every advancement has confirmed and substantiated the statements made by the literary and professional gentlemen who entrusted the publication of their observations to me. The Appendix, which contains these observations, is still included, though it has been enlarged by additional notes and letters that will surely increase the interest of that part of the work.

It will be noticed that the views and opinions of these gentlemen vary; this is not something to be regretted, as their facts are in harmony. Their character ensures respect. No person possessing common honesty or a decent sense of propriety would go out and report that few scientific men in this area believe in <term>Mesmerism</term>.

The character of Dr. Charles Poyen, who introduced the subject to this country, was naturally viewed with suspicion and misunderstood by many; yet the complete success of the enterprise he began has removed any reason for suspicion and any excuse for misunderstanding. He worked zealously and unselfishly, and always conducted himself in such

<summary>The translator notes that the expansion of Mesmerism has validated previous observations and defends the integrity of the scientific men and Dr. Charles Poyen who promoted the practice. The updated edition includes an enlarged Appendix with further supporting evidence and letters.</summary>

Since no great effort was made to distribute the first edition of this work, several small, inexpensive, and poorly compiled works have been published in various places. These contain instructions primarily derived from Deleuze without acknowledgment, mixed with rules that are either questionable or absolutely harmful in their effect. # LIFE OF DELEUZE.

The life of the author of this work was translated by a lady from the detailed volume of Doctor Foissac. Anyone who reads it will find their confidence irresistibly drawn toward him by the evidence of a character in whom it is delightful to trust. Whatever our opinion of Mesmerism may be—which Deleuze has practiced gratuitously for more than half a century—we cannot refuse to grant him sincerity of mind and uprightness of intention. His various works indicate a careful and scrutinizing spirit, guided by a single-mindedness that rarely leads into harmful error. We trust in him as a guide because we see his caution; even if he does not bring conviction to his theory, he removes suspicion from his motives. And he is little to be envied who allows a common prejudice to influence his judgment when a subject of the highest importance, supported by the practice and testimony of Deleuze, demands a serious and careful investigation from him as a professional man.

**JOSEPH PHILIP FRANCIS DELEUZE** was born at Sisteron, Lower Alps, in March 1753. Desiring to pursue a military career, he came to Paris in 1772, intending to study mathematics; but since the appointments had not yet taken place, he entered the infantry with the rank of sub-lieutenant. Three years later, after the corps in which he served was disbanded, he left the service and devoted himself to the study of the natural sciences. While living in the country near Sisteron in 1785, he read for the first time an account of the cures performed at Buzancy, in which he placed no confidence; indeed, he suspected them to be fabrications designed to bring ridicule upon the supporters of Magnetism. But hearing that one

# LIFE OF DELEUZE.

of his friends (M. D. d'Aix), a man of cool reason and an enlightened mind, had been to see Mesmer at M. Servan's, and on his return to Aix had succeeded in producing somnambulism, he resolved to visit him and ascertain the truth.

"I performed the journey on foot," he said, "botanizing as I went, and arrived at Aix at noon on the second day, having walked since four o'clock in the morning. I immediately shared the purpose of my journey with my friend, asking him to tell me what he thought of the prodigies I had heard about; he smiled and said coolly, 'Wait and see for yourself; the patient will be here in three hours.'

"At the end of that time she arrived, accompanied by several people who were to form a chain. I joined this chain, and in a few minutes, I saw the patient fall asleep. I watched with astonishment, but falling asleep myself in less than fifteen minutes, I ceased to observe. During my sleep, I talked a great deal and was so excited that I disrupted the chain. I had no memory of this when I awoke and found them all laughing around me. The next day, instead of sleeping myself, I observed others and asked my friend to teach me the methods. On my return home, I attempted to magnetize the sick who lived in the neighboring villages. I was careful not to excite their imaginations, touching them under various pretexts and trying to convince them of the healing effect of gentle rubbing. In this way, I obtained some very curious and beneficial results, which strengthened my own faith. In the autumn, while in the city, I applied to a young physician—a man of much merit who combined the wisdom of healthy doubt with the desire to be convinced by actual experience. I requested that he find a patient for me, and if I effected a cure, he might consider this conclusive proof; I suggested at the same time that the subject should not be in a critical state, lest fatal consequences might follow from my inexperience. He introduced me to a young woman who had been sick for seven years, constantly suffering great pain and being much bloated; she also had a visible external swelling caused by a great enlargement of the spleen, which she showed to us. She was not able to walk or lie down. I succeeded in removing the obstruction, her circulation was restored, the

# LIFE OF DELEUZE.

The swelling gradually disappeared, and she was able to attend to her usual duties. When I touched her, she slept, but she did not become a somnambulist. Soon after, an intimate friend of mine (Mr. D.) magnetized a young girl of sixteen who became a somnambulist. She was the daughter of very respectable parents. I assisted in the treatment of this patient, and I have never known a more perfect somnambulist. She prescribed remedies for other sick persons as well as for herself. She displayed most of the phenomena observed by M. de Puysegur, M. Tardy, and the members of the society at Strasburg. Among these were phenomena I could not have imagined or explained. I can only affirm that I saw them, and after this, it is impossible for me to suspect even the slightest illusion or the possibility of deception.”

From this time, M. Deleuze missed no opportunity to gather and observe facts, relieving and curing a great number of people. Two years later, in 1787, he returned to Paris and pursued literature, science, philosophy, and particularly botany with renewed passion. In 1798, he was chosen as an assistant naturalist at the Garden of Plants; and when the professors belonging to the establishment joined together in 1802 to publish the *Annals of the Museum of Natural History*, he was appointed secretary of that association.*

M. Deleuze was first known to the learned world by his translation of *“Darwin’s Loves of the Plants”* in 1799, and *“Thompson’s Seasons”* in 1801–1806, at which time he published his *“Eudoxus, or Conversations on the Study of the Sciences, Letters, and Philosophy,”* 2 vols. 8vo; Paris, 1810. The varied knowledge displayed in his writings, the soundness of his doctrines, his excellent judgment, and his style—so clear, simple, and yet elegant—place him among writers of the first rank. His book, the best of those intended for the instruction of the young, has received the most flattering and honorable praise from the learned.

Plants, he did not neglect this new order of physiological phenomena, which had been despised by scholars until now. He did not say, like Fontenelle and others, "If I had my hand full of truth, I should be careful how I opened it;" instead, during the furious contest occurring between the supporters and the enemies of Magnetism, he was content to observe in silence. He waited until the excitement was over to publish his "*Critical History of Magnetism*," the result of twenty-nine years of investigation and reflection. 

This work appeared in 1813, marking an era in the annals of science, and is now translated into all the principal languages of Europe. In this work, he took a different course from those who had preceded him. "I shall not," he said, "permit myself to form any hypothesis, but shall state what has been witnessed by myself and by men worthy of credit." After a general sketch of the history of the discovery and the obstacles opposed to it, he devotes a very remarkable article to the examination of the proofs on which the new doctrine is founded. 

He first lays down principles of indisputable correctness concerning the probability of testimony and applies them with equal logic and wisdom to the examination of the proofs of Magnetism. He shows that its effects have been attested by thousands of witnesses, among whom are found physicians, scholars, and enlightened men who have not been afraid to face ridicule in obeying the voice of conscience and fulfilling a duty to humanity. He notes that those who have published their opinions—and the far larger number who make their observations in silence and content themselves with admitting their belief when questioned on the subject—have all either witnessed or actually produced the phenomena of which they speak. Meanwhile, among the adversaries of Magnetism, not a single man can be found who has examined the subject in the only proper way: by experimenting for himself with the most scrupulous attention and in exact accordance with the prescribed directions.

With the same powerful reasoning, he has treated the means by which Magnetism acts, the methods of producing it, and the influence that the faith of the patients and the comparative power of magnetizers may have upon the efficacy of the treatment. The second volume of the “Critical History” fully justifies the title of the work. It is devoted to an analysis and examination of the writings which have been published concerning Magnetism, of which there are nearly three hundred. M. Deleuze has fulfilled this difficult task with great discernment. His research shows that the opponents of Magnetism have tried in vain to shake the foundation of the doctrine and the authenticity of the facts on which it rests. “It should be concluded,” he says in closing, “that the science of Magnetism should be associated with the other branches of human knowledge; that after having proved the existence of the agent, we should ascertain the part it plays in the operations of nature; and having classified its facts according to their degrees of probability, we should place them beside the other phenomena of physiology, so that we may decide whether they depend upon a new principle, or upon a modification of one already known.”

We would know little of M. Deleuze if we supposed for an instant that he takes advantage of his position to hurl back the ridicule and contempt with which they wished to overwhelm him. To this strange demand, M. Deleuze contented himself with replying: "Everyone knows very well that M. Virey will never be convinced if he must first witness such a phenomenon as this."

After having addressed the learned world in his "*Critical History*," M. Deleuze wished to draw up a system of rules which should place the subject within the reach of all minds. This end he has attained by publishing his "*Practical Instruction*," Paris, 1825. Men well-versed in its phenomena will find in this book the results of a lifetime of experience. His rare qualities and his pleasant and instructive conversation have gained him many friends among the most celebrated scholars, including Levaillant, Duperron, Cuvier, de Humboldt, and others. In the unanimous opinion of his contemporaries, he shares with the Marquis de Puysegur the honor of having defended and spread one of the most beautiful discoveries of modern times.

## INTRODUCTION.

Several people have requested that I publish plain and simple instructions on the subject of Magnetism, free from all theory and suitable in all cases to guide those who are convinced of the reality of the agent, and who are at a loss for how to make use of it. I am now going to fulfill this task, solely with the goal of being useful.

It is not the object of this work to convince men who, though otherwise well-informed, still doubt the reality of Magnetism; it is intended chiefly for those who are not engaged in medicine, physiology, or physics, who believe based on oral testimony without having seen any person magnetized, and who, being persuaded that I know more than themselves on the subject, wish to try my method in order to succeed—as I have had the happiness of doing—in curing and relieving the ailments of their fellow creatures. I shall lay down principles which I believe to be true, without entering into any discussion to prove their truth. I shall avoid pronouncing upon that which appears doubtful; and if I sometimes err in the mode of explaining things, my errors, pertaining solely to the theory which I have adopted to connect the phenomena by referring them to the same cause, will not affect the indi-

* *This was written in 1825.* Since that time, in 1831, the <term>Royal Academy of Medicine</term>, through its committee—whose report is worthy of study as a model of precise philosophical investigation—delivered an opinion on the subject that has changed public feeling in France regarding it. Its existence, as a special faculty of the human mind, is no longer a matter of doubt among scientists who have witnessed its phenomena. The extent of its usefulness is now a question worthy of deep investigation, and not to be settled by people who never think and who decide without looking into its merits. Theses on <term>Mesmerism</term> have been written in Paris by candidates for medical degrees; one of these, in 1842, was dedicated to Professor <term>Orfila</term>, Dean of the Medical Academy. <term>Orfila</term> and <term>Arago</term>—names which France has reason to be proud of—have dedicated attention to this subject. The former, upon witnessing some of its results, declared that they ought to be *proclaimed to the world from the top of the <term>French Institute</term>*. <term>Dr. Lordat</term>, in his recent work on Human Physiology, assigns it a high place among the phenomena belonging to man's biological organization. The evidence in favor of its usefulness is so abundant in highly authoritative European works that an ignorance of its true history (which is not to be found in the encyclopedias) may be considered strange in well-informed people, and disgraceful if they allow themselves to oppose it through a prejudice born of a lack of curiosity. In this area, it receives the support of medical practitioners of undeniable skill. It should always be in the hands of such experts, or administered under their direction. To promote this goal, and to redirect public attention from curious phenomena to its true use, the translator has provided an English version of the instructions of the venerable <term>Deleuze</term>.

# ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

## CHAPTER I.

### *GENERAL VIEWS AND PRINCIPLES.*

1. Man has the faculty of exercising a beneficial influence over his fellow men by directing the vital principle toward them through his will.
2. The name of Magnetism has been given to this faculty; it is an extension of the power which all living beings have of acting upon those who are subjected to their will.
3. We perceive this faculty only by its results, and we make no use of it except as far as we will to use it.
4. The first condition of action, then, is to exercise the will.
5. As we cannot comprehend how one body can act upon another at a distance without there being something to establish a communication between them, we suppose that a substance emanates from the person who magnetizes and is conveyed to the person magnetized in the direction given to it by the will. This substance, which sustains life in us, we call the magnetic fluid. The nature of this fluid is unknown; even its exist-

7. If the will is necessary to direct the fluid, belief is necessary to lead one to make a firm and steady use of the faculties he possesses. Confidence in the power we possess makes us act without effort and without distraction. As for the rest, confidence is only the consequence of belief: it differs in this only—one believes *himself* to be endowed with a power whose reality he does not doubt.

8. In order for one individual to act upon another, there must exist between them a moral and physical sympathy, just as there is between all the members of a living body. Physical sympathy is established by methods which we shall point out; moral sympathy is established by the desire to do good to someone who wishes to receive it, or by ideas and desires which, occupying them both equally, form a communication of feelings between them. When this sympathy is well established between two individuals, we say they are in communication.

Magnetism does nothing more than employ, regulate, and direct the forces of nature. The more the course of nature has been interrupted by outside agents, the more difficult it is for the magnetizer to re-establish it. Magnetism, therefore, cures children and people who reside in the country much more promptly and effectively than those who have lived in the social world, who have taken much medicine, and whose nerves are irritated. ## *OF THE PROCESSES IN ANIMAL MAGNETISM.*

The principles we have given in the preceding chapter are essential and invariable; in all cases, the power and effectiveness of Magnetism depend upon their application. The processes of which we are about to speak are not used in the same way by all magnetizers. Many of them follow unique ones; but, whatever method they pursue, the results are nearly the same. The processes, however, should be varied according to circumstances. We are often determined in the choice not only by the type of disease, but by a regard for convenience and other circumstances, and even by the desire to avoid what might appear extraordinary. ### PROCESSES IN ANIMAL MAGNETISM. ###

I think it is proper to distinguish the passes that are made without touching from those made with touch—not only with the fingertips but with the entire surface of the hand, while applying slight pressure at the same time. I call these last ones *magnetic frictions*. They are often used to act more effectively upon the arms, the legs, and the back, along the vertebral column.

This method of magnetizing by longitudinal passes—directing the fluid from the head to the extremities without focusing on any one part in preference to others—is called magnetizing by the long pass (*magnetisér à grands courans*). It is more or less appropriate in all cases, and it is necessary to use it in the first session when there is no special reason for using any other.

The fluid is thus distributed to all the organs, and it naturally accumulates in those that have need of it. In addition to the passes made at a short distance, others are made just before finishing at a distance of two or three feet. These generally produce a calm, refreshing, and pleasant sensation.

There is one more process with which it is very advantageous to end the session. It consists of standing by the side of the patient as they stand up and, at a distance of a foot, making seven or eight passes with both hands—one in front of the body and the other behind—starting above the head and descending to the floor, where the hands are then spread apart. This process clears the head, restores equilibrium, and provides strength.

### NOTE III.

A short time after Mesmer, who explained all the phenomena of <term>Magnetism</term> by causes purely physical, some persons, going into the opposite extreme, substituted a system of spiritualism in the place of this theory. *M. le Chevalier de Barbarin*, a very pious man, but probably too much devoted to mystical ideas, claimed that all processes were useless, and that faith and the will were sufficient to perform wonders. Those who adopted his opinions resorted to prayers at the patients’ bedsides, and often succeeded in curing them. The success they obtained proves nothing to support their principles; and the state of concentration which this method demands might give rise to bad consequences. Our spirit is the source of voluntary movements; it gives impulse to the <term>nervous fluid</term>; but so long as it is united to organized matter, it is destined to act externally, by the aid of the organs, either immediately, or by the emanation which is carried to a distance, like the rays from a luminous body. I have refrained from all theory, and I would have been silent upon the opinions of the spiritualists, if there were not at this time men of good intentions, who, disdaining <term>Magnetism</term>, undertake to treat patients by practices which they think more powerful and more efficacious. They obtain cures, undoubtedly; they produce <term>ecstatic somnambulism</term>; and their somnambulists are persuaded they are inspired. This may lead into errors, and disturb the imagination not only of the patients, but also of those who consult them. Let anyone recall the singular ideas entertained by those who witnessed the somnambulists of Sweden, and he will see that nothing can be more contrary to reason. Let us not, then, consider <term>somnambulism</term> as a supernatural state, in which

# CHAPTER III.

## *OF THE EFFECTS AND THEIR INDICATIONS.*

### Of the Effects by which the Action of Magnetism is manifested, and of the Modifications which the Observation of these Effects indicates in the Processes.

There are some patients upon whom Magnetism does not act, owing either to a peculiarity of constitution, to the kind of disease, or to a lack of rapport with the magnetizer; but this is very rare. It is less rare that the connection cannot be established until after several sessions; for this reason, one cannot assume that Magnetism is not working until after a trial of five days.

To justify this assumption, even after this period has passed, it is not enough that the patient has felt nothing when you have attempted to magnetize him. It must be considered whether he has experienced no change in his condition; whether he does not find himself better, or whether his disease has not been prevented from worsening according to its ordinary course. It frequently happens that Magnetism gradually re-establishes the harmony of the system without producing any physical sensation, and its influence is perceived only in the restoration of health. them. I will now explain what is meant by crises:

Physicians give the name of *crisis* to every sudden change which, occurring during a disease, modifies its progress or character and enables us to foresee its result.

These crises appear to be nature's effort to free itself of the <term>morbific principle</term>. They are beneficial when they operate completely; they are harmful when the patient does not have the strength to endure them. They are manifested by symptoms such as a shift in the location of the malady, a remarkable change in the pulse, evacuations, excretions, eruptions, the gathering of <term>humors</term>, pains in certain parts, nervous movements, etc. In acute diseases, these crises generally occur on specific days, which are called the *critical days*.

Mesmer says there are no cures without crises. If by this he meant that the patient does not recover his health except by a change of state, it is so obvious that it requires no further comment. If he meant that the cure is achieved by a sudden change manifested by obvious symptoms, it is not always true; for many diseases are cured by slow and gradual improvement, without anyone being able to mark the moment when they assumed a favorable character. A fever diminishes day by day and entirely ceases, and a hundred other diseases are soothed and disappear when no one can determine the cause of the cessation any more than that of the attack. But it is true that, in most acute diseases, the cure takes place by an evident change which occurs all at once in the state of the patient.

Magnetizers have given the name of *crises* to the remarkable changes which the action of Magnetism produces upon those who are subjected to it, or to

The term *magnetic state* has been given to every state different from the natural one that results from the magnetic influence. This term is more general than the word *crisis* and is not ambiguous.

Among the effects of the magnetic treatment, there is one of which it is proper to be forewarned, and which I omitted to mention. I will now supply that omission.

## CHAPTER IV.

### *OF THE ACCESSORY MEANS TO INCREASE THE MAGNETIC ACTION, AND OF THOSE BY WHICH THE DIRECT ACTION IS SUPPLIED.*

The magnetizer can transmit his fluid to many objects, and these objects become either the conductors of his action or suitable instruments for its transmission, producing magnetic effects on people with whom he is in communication. By using one of these auxiliaries, he can also conduct the treatment of many patients at the same time without exhausting himself, provided they are not somnambulists.

These auxiliaries include magnetized water, woolen and cotton cloth, glass plates, etc., as well as magnetized trees and magnetic troughs or reservoirs. The chain—the joining together of many people holding hands in harmony under the direction of one magnetizer—is also among the auxiliary means.

Magnetized water is one of the most powerful and beneficial agents that can be used. Once communication is established, patients are made to drink it, either during or between their meals. It carries the magnetic fluid directly into the stomach and from there into all the organs. It facilitates the crisis to which nature is inclined, and, therefore, sometimes

The <term>baquet</term> and the <term>chain</term> have often been used at the same time. This is done after arranging the patients around the reservoir. They are directed to form a <term>chain</term>. For the following reasons, I do not approve of this method:

When several patients meet around the *<term>baquet</term>*, it is for the purpose of receiving the action of the <term>magnetic fluid</term> concentrated there, without any direct communication between them; but when a <term>chain</term> is formed, it is so that the patient may receive the influence of all the persons who compose it; from this it follows that all of them ought to be in good health. These two means should, therefore, be used separately and in different circumstances: they do not suit all patients equally, and each one has its advantages and its disadvantages. This subject requires a few additional observations.

Although the *<term>baquet</term>* has a milder and slower action than direct manipulation, people suffering from severe diseases, which do not arise from morbid inaction, are exposed to <term>crises</term> which should be calmed separately. When these <term>crises</term> occur, they may influence the other patients and even be communicated by sympathy or by imitation. We know how violent these <term>crises</term> may become when we remember how they were in the time of <term>Mesmer</term>. It is true that we did not then understand how to calm them, and the same accidents did not take place at <term>Strasburg</term>; yet it is always proper to take precautions; and if you assemble a large number around the *<term>baquet</term>*, it is necessary to have several <term>magnetizers</term>, and one of them should have an acquaintance with medicine. Some have occasionally employed iron <term>wands</term> artificially magnetized, like the compass needle; and they think that they act with more power; but they certainly do not agree with all patients. I do not recommend them. The <term>wand</term> is designed to direct and concentrate the <term>magnetic fluid</term>, and not to modify it by a foreign influence.

The <term>magnetizer</term> who makes use of the <term>wand</term> ought to have one of his own and not lend it to any person, lest it should be charged with different fluids—a precaution more important than it is commonly thought to be.

# CHAPTER V.

->*OF SOMNAMBULISM, AND OF THE USE TO BE MADE OF IT.*<-

It is a well-known fact that certain people walk, speak, and act in their sleep, and that when they are awakened, they have no memory of what they have been doing. These people are called <term>somnambulists</term>—that is, sleep-walkers—and the state in which they are is called <term>somnambulism</term>. The tendency to walk in one's sleep has been considered a nervous condition which we should try to counteract because of the accidents which might result from it.

The apparent resemblance between spontaneous <term>somnambulism</term> and the crises which are often produced by <term>Magnetism</term> has led men to call the latter *magnetic somnambulism*. A more appropriate name might have been found; but as this has been accepted for forty years, it is useless to change it.

<term>Magnetic somnambulism</term>, which we call simply <term>somnambulism</term>—because that term cannot be ambiguous in this work—is a state of existence during which the person who is in it appears to be asleep. If his <term>magnetizers</term> speak to him, he answers without waking; he can also perform various movements, and when he returns to the natural state, he retains no memory of what has passed. His eyes are closed; he generally understands only those who are put in communication with him. The external organs of sense

Somnambulism presents infinitely varied phenomena. Descriptions of them may be found in a great number of works published on this subject. This is not the place to describe them. My goal is solely to teach the means of obtaining the most useful results from this crisis, without exposing oneself to the slightest inconvenience.

Of all the discoveries that have excited attention since the remotest antiquity, that of somnambulism certainly gives us the most insight into the nature and the faculties of man. The phenomena to which it has drawn our attention demonstrate the distinction between two things: the twofold existence of the internal and the external man in a single individual. They offer direct proof of the spirituality of the soul and an answer to all the objections raised against its immortality. It was impossible that those who devoted themselves to the practice of Magnetism should not be struck, sooner or later, by a phenomenon which was bound to present itself. It was equally impossible that they should not have been seized with enthusiasm at the sight of the wonderful things which accompany it, and kept it a secret. It was, finally, impossible that men who were strangers to the true principles of Magnetism would not seek to produce these same wonderful things to exercise their power and satisfy their curiosity, and yet know how to keep themselves within proper bounds to avoid dangers and errors. As a result, Magnetism has often been employed, not to cure diseases, but to induce somnambulism. And because somnambulists have faculties and means of knowledge that we do not possess, people have imagined they must know everything and have consulted them as oracles. If, instead of yielding to enthusiasm, they had examined the phenomena through the light of physiology, they would have perceived the danger of pushing a state too far during which an inexplicable change occurs in the functions of the nervous system, in the activity of the organs, and in the way sensation is perceived and transmitted. They would have seen that the more the sensibility is heightened, the more they ought to be on guard against what might increase that intensity; that at the very limit of the path nature has marked out for herself—and which she has the strength to follow while preserving the harmony of all faculties and the control of reason—an immense field is opened to the imagination, where illusions take the place of truth. They would have seen that somnambulism is only a transient crisis, which must be utilized without wandering from the

<term>Somnambulism</term> is well known; it presents itself often in magnetic practice; let us see what the means are of always deriving the greatest advantage from it and avoiding all misuse of it.

The first advice I shall give is that you never seek to produce <term>somnambulism</term>, but rather let it come naturally, in order to profit by it when it occurs.

Many magnetizers, in order to produce it, focus too much on the head; and, by this means, they often succeed in obtaining a forced sleep, a rush of blood toward the brain, and partial crises, which are of no use. This method is not without danger. It is much better simply to employ <term>Magnetism</term> by the <term>long pass</term>, and not to focus on the head more than the other parts of the body. If nature is inclined toward this crisis, the <term>fluid</term> will, of itself, be carried to the brain, and the tendency toward <term>somnambulism</term> will be manifested by the patient being in a state of tranquility, by his closing his eyes, and by his sleeping. You may then, without any inconvenience, pass your fingertips five or six times at a short distance before his eyes, in order to deepen his sleep.

You may then ask him how he is, or whether he sleeps well. Then one of these three things will take place—he will wake up, he will not answer, or he will answer.

If you are alone with a <term>somnambulist</term>, and anyone is permitted to enter, the <term>somnambulist</term> generally perceives it. Sometimes the person who enters is indifferent to him; at other times he feels for them either a sympathy or an antipathy. In either case, it diminishes his <term>concentrativeness</term>. If he feels sympathy, his attention is divided; if he feels antipathy, he suffers. If the stranger is incredulous and suspects the sincerity of the <term>somnambulist</term>, or makes a joke of what he sees, the <term>somnambulist</term> is troubled and loses his <term>lucidity</term>. If many witnesses surround the <term>somnambulist</term> and are occupied with him, the <term>fluid</term> of each one of them acts upon his organization; and, as these various <term>fluids</term> are not in harmony, he experiences discordant effects from them. If you have around you only the persons who desire the cure of the patient, and if you <term>magnetize</term> them all to put them in <term>communication</term>, and all are in good health, the <term>somnambulist</term> may not be in the least disquieted. But it will be difficult to prevent many of the spectators from often occupying themselves with other things besides the patient. For every time they occupy themselves with something else, they will break the <term>communication</term>; and these interruptions produce shocks (*secousses*), which disturb the tranquil state of <term>somnambulism</term>. There is sometimes among the spectators someone who inspires the <term>somnambulist</term> with a particular affection of the most exalted kind; and that would turn him aside from his attention to himself. With the will of the <term>magnetizer</term> no longer active, he does not exert the same control, and the <term>somnambulism</term> takes on an irregular character.

# OF <term>SOMNAMBULISM</term>.

The greater part of <term>somnambulists</term>, even in the hands of good <term>magnetizers</term>, have lost a portion of their faculties, because many persons in succession have been permitted to see them.

At the close of the preceding chapter, I said that, in a <term>magnetic treatment</term>, there ought to be only one will active, to which all others ought to be subordinate. This rule is especially to be observed when you have <term>somnambulists</term>: <term>M. de Puységur</term> has not failed to call attention to this; and yet many well-informed <term>magnetizers</term> do not pay sufficient regard to it. As to those who try it for the first time, it is almost impossible that they should feel the importance of it, and that even the desire of enlightening themselves upon the means of doing more good should not mislead them from the path which would conduct the most surely to the accomplishment of their object.

It is proper to enter into some details upon this head.

When a person, who has no experience, obtains for the first time some of the singular effects which generally precede <term>lucid somnambulism</term>, he thinks it would be useful to get acquainted with an experienced <term>magnetizer</term>. If he finds one, he entreats him to come and assist at the sittings, to give him instructions. ### OF SOMNAMBULISM.

My young somnambulist, who had displayed the most extraordinary clairvoyance for several days, ceased to manifest his various faculties, suddenly acquiring only the ability to express himself through words, and made no further progress afterwards. May the instruction I now give help others avoid the many mistakes I made before I gained my own experience!

I could go into many details here regarding the essential character of somnambulism, the general causes of its countless variations, the distinction between the states of wakefulness, sleep, and delirium, and the transitions from one state to another; but I have decided to refrain from all theory and limit myself to providing rules which I believe to be correct, without explaining my reasons for adopting them. I will then simply say:

If your patient becomes a somnambulist, keep near you only the witness you admitted at the start, who is in communication with you. Absolutely refuse to show him to any curious person, and let no one approach him except when it is useful, and with the precautions I will soon describe. Ask him no questions except those relating to his health, and pace these questions so as not to fatigue him. Do not look for amazing effects; by all means, refrain from describing those you have already seen. You can allow yourself that satisfaction when the treatment is finished; but until then, you should think only of the cure.

Before introducing a patient to your somnambulist, you will let him touch something that the patient has worn, so that he may tell you whether he feels any repugnance toward it, and whether he sees any danger in being put in communication with him. You will not allow your somnambulist to be magnetized indiscriminately by any person. Those somnambulists who are in communication with several magnetizers end up losing their lucidity.

If essential business forces you to interrupt the treatment of your somnambulist, reach an understanding with him to find someone to take your place. Should the interruption be for only a few days, the magnetizer taking your place should act only in your name, according to your views and your method, and under your direction. If the interruption is to be of long duration, you should give up your somnambulist entirely.

If your somnambulist has whims, you will oppose them by letting him know your will, without dispute. Never allow him to get the upper hand over you. You ought to yield to everything that will lead to his well-being, and resist his fantastic notions. You are for him an attentive and benevolent, but just and inflexible, providence.

I return to the method of applying the procedures once somnambulism has been induced.

The somnambulist always indicates the procedures that are appropriate for him, so there can be no uncertainty about them. These procedures are sometimes very laborious and very tiring for the magnetizer; they demand patience, courage, and devotion. Most of the time, nature works alone during somnambulism, and you do not need to do anything more than hold the somnambulist’s thumbs, place your hand on his knees, or even simply attend to him.

You do not need to magnetize him longer than he deems useful, on the days and at the hours he indicates. While it is essential not to interrupt a crisis when it begins, it is often harmful to prolong it beyond the required time.

# OF SOMNAMBULISM.

There are somnambulists who fear the effect of light that is too strong. I have seen some of them who had their eyes bandaged; but there are others who feel strain from closing their eyelids and who request to have their eyes opened. The magnetizer succeeds in doing this by making passes across the eyes without diminishing the intensity of the somnambulism. The somnambulist then seems to be in his natural state; but it is necessary to watch over him according to the precautions he indicates. There are cases when this non-apparent somnambulism can be very useful, as we shall soon see.

When we wish to ask the somnambulist a question, it is necessary to express our will through words. Good somnambulists understand the will without our speaking to them. But why should we use this method when there is no need for it? It is an experiment; and it is a rule that everyone ought to adopt: to prohibit all experimentation. I agree that there are cases where it is beneficial to use only the influence of the will. For instance, there may be a third person near you, and you perceive that your somnambulist—who thinks he is alone with you—is about to say things which this third person ought not to know; you will impose silence by your will.

# OF <term>SOMNAMBULISM</term>.

When I commenced writing this chapter, I did not plan to go any further.* I resolved to pass over the extraordinary phenomena in silence. I thought that those who had not seen similar things would view me as a dreamer, and that such a reputation would not only be distressing to me, but might also create obstacles to doing the good I wish to do. After all, people will be guided by the advice of a man prone to illusions no more than they would follow a man lacking good faith. But after reflecting on it, I thought it my duty to yield to more important considerations and to rise above the fears caused by my own pride. I am determined, then, to speak of a very singular state, because others may encounter it just as I and many of my friends have. It is important to know this state so that it is not confused with the "exaltation" whose dangers I have already pointed out, and so that its development is not hindered.

I am first going to describe the type of <term>somnambulism</term> I wish to discuss. I will then explain how one should behave with those who have reached that state, if one wishes to gain any benefit from it, for them or for oneself.

### NOTE I.

I have stated that <term>somnambulists</term> do not every day exhibit the same degree of <term>clairvoyance</term>; but I forgot to mention that they sometimes lose it in respect to this or that patient with whom they have long been in communication, while at the same time they show a great deal of it in relation to others. This anomaly is unusual, but I have, unfortunately, seen many instances of it. I will explain.

In severe chronic diseases, it happens very frequently that, at the first consultation, the <term>somnambulist</term> sees, in an astonishing manner, the previous state and the current state of the patient. He points out the remedies which first produce relief, and, some days later, such an improvement as to make us consider the cure as certain. Everything he says is realized, and our confidence appears to be well founded. But afterward, the condition of the patient changes. He grows worse. The <term>somnambulist</term> continues to prescribe remedies which do not produce the intended effects. He no

### NOTE II.

The Treatise on <term>Somnambulism</term> published by Doctor Bertrand is the first work, *ex professo* <note>as a professional expert</note>, upon the subject, and the only one in which it has been examined in its numerous relations. I showed him some facts, and his old prejudices did not prevent him from yielding to the evidence. His wife has many times helped him save patients for whom the resources of his medical art seemed insufficient to him.

Unfortunately, Madame de Montaux is in delicate health; her physical strength does not match her moral energy, and the practice of <term>Magnetism</term> causes a fatigue that she is always too late in noticing. After treating a malignant fever—which she cured by combining <term>Magnetism</term> with medicinal remedies at her husband's request—I saw her so ill that she could hardly have been restored without being magnetized herself. One very extraordinary thing, which I cannot account for, is that she commonly takes on the disease of the person she magnetizes; not that the *cause* of the disease passes to her, but that she experiences its sensations and symptoms for several days. I have seen an instance of this during an attack of the <term>gout</term> and in an <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note>, which are not contagious diseases.

By reflecting on the effects she produced and those she experienced, Madame de Montaux discovered the principles of <term>Magnetism</term> for herself, and she has drawn the most useful results from them. She has written down her observations and shown me her manuscript, from which I have profited. In it, I found very accurate remarks, a singleness of purpose, and, above all, a love of order and a zeal for doing good. This is the same character observed in the work she published under the title of ‘*Moral and Political Reflections upon the Advantages of Monarchy*.’ ”

If you continue after being cured, or even after having obtained from <term>Magnetism</term> all the good it can effect, you will become habituated to it; and this is a great inconvenience to persons sensitive to its action, and especially to those who are susceptible to <term>somnambulism</term>.

Although <term>Magnetism</term> consists in the influence exercised by one individual over another, many <term>magnetizers</term> think that one can magnetize oneself; it is true, but only in regard to certain persons and certain cases.

When a man, in the habit of magnetizing, has a local pain—for example, in the arm, the leg, or the stomach—he can dissipate or relieve it by attentively employing the <term>magnetic processes</term> on himself. But to do this, he must be in good health. When a person has a general disease, a fever, or an organic affection, it is plain that he cannot draw the remedy from himself, since the fluid of which he makes use no longer has the necessary qualities.

Among the persons who have been magnetized many times, there are some who can, of their own accord, throw themselves into the <term>magnetic state</term>. I believe this is a faculty they ought never to employ; because, by exercising it, they acquire the habit of <term>concentration</term>, which may fatigue the <term>nervous system</term> and become very injurious, as we shall say when we come to speak of the dangers of <term>Magnetism</term>.

I believe I should not finish this chapter without answering a question often addressed to me.

In the present state of things, say some persons, <term>Magnetism</term> is so little known that many patients cannot find, either in their family or among their friends, anyone who is able or willing to magnetize them.

## NOTE A.

Some individuals possess a truly prodigious magnetic power; while I do not claim to know its cause, I think it is my duty to say a word about it. First, I request those who are naturally endowed with it to use it without ostentation and without trying to produce astonishing effects, but with simplicity, prudence, and solely with the goal of doing good. Second, I say this so that, under certain circumstances, people may seek out those of whom they have heard rumors of marvelous cures. Third, I say this so that they may be satisfied with the specific and limited nature of the power I am referring to; for someone who can perform certain actions may not succeed in obtaining other, equally surprising effects of a different kind.

For instance, many magnetizers induce somnambulism with great ease and do not expect success except through this crisis, while others can barely achieve it and yet do just as much good. Some of them cure only certain diseases; others soothe or cure all curable illnesses alike. Some act only through their will, without any visible magnetic process, and they can even exert this influence from a distance. They put themselves in communication with the patient who seeks their help by aligning their intentions with them and through the exchange of thoughts and feelings. Finally, magnetizers have been known who, despite possessing extraordinary power, use it only to produce astonishing phenomena that serve no useful purpose. These individuals expose magnetism to ridicule; they drive wise people away from the subject and provide ammunition to those who consider it dangerous. I cannot emphasize too much...

He devoted some minutes to each of them to direct the fluid; he soothed those who experienced crises by taking them aside from the rest. But, despite his desire to accomplish it, he never produced complete somnambulism. Moreover, he went to the houses of the sick who could not leave their homes.

Things were in this state when he came to find me, to tell me what he had done and to ask my advice. Although he expressed himself with the greatest simplicity, what he related appeared so extraordinary to me that I desired to verify the facts. I went to spend two days with him at his house. I conversed with the patients whom he had cured, and with those who were under treatment. I advised him to substitute a dry *baquet*, in which bottles filled with magnetized water should be placed, for his *baquet* filled with water; and, three months later, I returned to spend three more days with him to find out the results obtained since my first visit.

I will not recount here the cures performed by this treatment; it will suffice to say that, among those subjected to it, many had long-standing diseases which had resisted medicinal remedies, and that the small number of those who were not restored to perfect health were considerably relieved.

But here is what may be considered even more remarkable. M. N—— is free from excessive enthusiasm, and he exerts a moral influence over his patients which matches the nature of his own spirit. All who place themselves around his *baquet* feel calm and pleasant sensations. Their imagination is never over-excited. They are attached to their magnetizer and take an interest in each other. ## CHAPTER VII.

### *OF THE APPLICATION OF MAGNETISM TO DISEASES, AND ITS CONNECTION WITH MEDICINE.*

From the time of Hippocrates to our own days, medicine has been practiced by men who have dedicated their lives to study, who have called to their aid all the natural and physical sciences, and who, endowed with the talent of observation and with tireless zeal, unite their own experience with that of their contemporaries and their predecessors. Countless facts have been collected, discussed, and compared. A solid foundation has been established in anatomy; in the knowledge of external signs that indicate the alterations of various organs; in the knowledge of the constant action that certain substances exert on the human body; in the comparison of the effects obtained by various modes of treatment; in the classification of diseases; and in some general principles, founded upon experience, in relation to which everyone agrees. And yet medicine is still uncertain. Although it has been taught in the schools for two thousand years, physicians do not agree either about the causes of diseases or the choice of proper remedies. The science has changed a hundred times since the days of Galen, and conflicting opinions have ruled successively in the schools. There is hardly a disease that has not

Some physicians have declared themselves for the medicine of the future; others, for medicine as it is. Some are for using few remedies; others advise having recourse to many. The most active medicines have been praised with enthusiasm or condemned as dangerous, according to their agreement with the doctrines of the leader of this or that school. Even today, when the science of medicine has been so well taught; when the most exact observations have been collected, classified, and compared; when pathological anatomy has arrived at the highest degree of perfection—physicians are still seen to differ in opinion regarding the use of bleeding, leeches, purgatives, and <term>Peruvian bark</term>, in this or that disease. The pupils of one master, who is undoubtedly very skillful, maintain that, up to his time, no one has properly understood medicine; while those of another school, acknowledging that he has shed great light upon the nature and the seat of many diseases, and confessing the success he has himself obtained by his method, consider him, nevertheless, a rash innovator whose principles, too broadly generalized, may be erroneous and dangerous.

I will here add a moral consideration, which I have set forth in my *Critical History*. It is this: If, in a dangerous illness, you rely upon Magnetism without consulting your physician, you take upon yourself a great responsibility; and if the patient dies, you will have cause for self-reproach. There are two great classes of diseases: <term>acute diseases</term>, which are rapid in their progress and which, once the dangers they exhibit during their development are overcome, terminate at a known period and are followed by <term>convalescence</term>; and <term>chronic diseases</term>, which are not limited in duration, whose course is uncertain, and whose crises and symptoms vary, without our having any certain means of judging the probability of a cure from them. A young man, twenty years old, became so insane that he was placed in a lunatic asylum. People whose minds are alienated are often known to experience pleasurable sensations in the presence of certain individuals who have a natural influence over them, and to whom they submit without resistance. These are the people who would most readily succeed in curing them. Those whose presence frightens or repels them will not accomplish it. It is probable that with most insane people whose fits are irregular, one might produce a soothing influence followed by sleep, and eventually by somnambulism*; then their restoration is almost certain. If the patient has a prevalent idea, the magnetizer may drive it away by an effort of the will. I know very well that the majority of trials of this kind would be fruitless; but here the matter is so important, and medicine has so few resources, that we should not neglect a means whose success is possible.

### NOTE.

A physician from the faculty of Paris has just sent me an observation that I think is useful to publish, because it relates to a disease I have not yet mentioned.

*Constant vertigo and accidental chorea cured by magnetism.*—Mademoiselle S——, age thirty-eight, experienced a violent fright on October 17th, which suddenly changed her condition by causing a suppression. Twenty-four hours later, there was heaviness in the lumbar region and the lower parts of the abdomen, headache, loss of appetite, and irregular movement in the arm and leg on the right side. These movements closely resembled Saint Vitus’s dance. For three months, the physician used all the appropriate remedies—leeches, sedatives, antispasmodics, sulfate of quinine, and so on. He believed the stomach and abdomen were improving; however, he could not succeed in clearing the vertigo, restoring the blood’s natural circulation, or calming the nervous movements. The patient, who was suffering greatly, asked whether magnetism might be useful in these circumstances. The physician advised her to try it. He stopped giving her medicines and recommended that she live temperately. They began magnetizing her in the middle of January, only three times a week, for twelve or fifteen minutes per session. The patient drank nothing but magnetized water. At the beginning of February, the nervous symptoms were gradually vanishing, and they had totally disappeared by the middle of the month. The patient regained her health and cheerfulness, her blood resumed its natural circulation, and by March her health was fully restored.

## CHAPTER VIII.

### *OF THE INCONVENIENCES, THE ABUSES AND THE DANGERS OF MAGNETISM, AND OF THE MEANS OF PREVENTING THEM.*

The opponents of Magnetism, after declaring that it does not exist, have spoken out against the dangers that accompany it. I will not stop to prove that what they have said of the processes employed to put it into action, and of the effects it produces, is very far from the truth, and that the anecdotes they have cited to make it appear hateful are entirely foreign to it. I agree that Magnetism has sometimes been abused and is still liable to be abused again. But a danger ceases to be important when we are warned of it and have easy and certain means of avoiding it. Magnetism is an agent of inconceivable power. Its usefulness depends upon the way in which it is employed; and in this, it is like fire, the use of which is not forbidden for fear of a conflagration.

Those who conform to the directions laid down in the preceding chapters will never have reason to fear the least inconvenience from the use of Magnetism. Yet, as many of my readers may not see the importance of the precautions I have recommended; as others may be alarmed by what has been said of the bad consequences of some treat-

Those who have wished to instill fear regarding the use of this agent as a curative treatment have based their observations on very plausible-sounding reasoning, which would be unfair if applied to ordinary medicine. Since magnetism has a very powerful effect, they have said that this action must be either beneficial or harmful, depending on the nature of the illness. If it is a tonic, it will increase the illness when there is too much excitement; if it is soothing, it can produce no good results in a sluggish state of the system.

In certain organic diseases that are very severe and long-standing, nature's efforts to take a new direction may produce the most painful and alarming crises. If the magnetizer becomes frightened and interrupts the action, the patient runs the risk of succumbing. In these cases, which are fortunately very rare, it would be necessary to have a somnambulist sufficiently clairvoyant to predict the crises, to describe the manner of their development, and the results they ought to achieve. The magnetizer would be equally reassured if he were directed by a physician knowledgeable in the study of magnetism. If this aid is lacking, I can only recommend confidence and courage. I have seen the interruption or the mismanagement of a treatment lead, over time, to the most fatal consequences; but I have never seen a serious accident follow a violent crisis when its development was not hindered.

Many people fear that magnetism excites nervous disturbances and even convulsions, because they remember the effects that were initially produced by Mesmer. But at the time when Mesmer first gathered patients around the *baquet*, he knew neither the means of directing the agent he employed nor how to calm the crises; and since 1784, with the true principles of magnetism being well known, the scenes that once caused such a stir are no longer repeated. However, it is useful to explain here in what cases nervous crises may occur and how all their inconveniences may be avoided.

Until now, I have spoken only of the dangers to which we are exposed when magnetizing, without precautions, persons who are not somnambulists. Those which spring from somnambulism are even greater. To avoid them, it is necessary to know them, and I will therefore point them out.

I have just said that a magnetizer whose health is fundamentally bad may communicate the disease to the person whom he magnetizes. This is especially to be feared in somnambulism. I have seen proof of it several times. I will merely relate a fact which struck me forcibly. A young lady, who for a long time had a very serious nervous disease, was magnetized by a family friend, who made her a somnambulist on the first day. She very soon had favorable crises, and her health appeared to be noticeably improved. She flattered herself with the prospect of obtaining a complete cure, when her magnetizer was attacked with an inflammation of the larynx. I will not return here to the accidents that may result from temporary imprudences; I confine myself to a succinct summary of what I have said on this subject. *Never interrupt a crisis. Do not allow your somnambulist to be touched by anyone who is not in communication with him. Do not put him in communication with anyone, except for some good purpose, and when he desires it. Avoid magnetizing him in the presence of many people. Occupy yourself solely with his health. Follow the processes which he indicates to you. Do not fatigue him with experiments. If you neglect these precautions, you will diminish his lucidity, retard his cure, and do him an injury.* Yet this injury may ordinarily be repaired by proper care; and the majority of magnetizers are not instructed on this point by their own experience.

The dangers of which I am about to speak are, fortunately, much less frequent. They are not caused by a momentary fault of the magnetizer, but by the abuse of his own power. They are, with some individuals, the natural consequences of somnambulism; and, as they are very serious and difficult to remedy, the magnetizer ought to conduct himself in such a manner as to prevent them without fail.

# ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

People who have been somnambulists for a long time have been known to retain, even after being restored to health, a nervous sensitivity that makes them highly impressionable; even the slightest magnetic action may cause them to relapse into an imperfect state of somnambulism. Some of them have been observed to remain habitually in a magnetic state. This is a great inconvenience, and you must avoid it by following these directions:

*Do not magnetize your somnambulist any longer than he tells you it is necessary. Never speak to him after he wakes up about what he said while in somnambulism.* In ending each session, relieve him of the fluid with which he is charged, and wake him completely, so that there is no halfway point between his ordinary state and the somnambulic state. As soon as your patient is cured, refrain entirely from the desire to preserve his somnambulic abilities; intend, on the contrary, that they cease, until a new illness makes them useful to him again. Somnambulists who are no longer ill are generally poor somnambulists, and the tendency toward somnambulism does not align with the ordinary habits of life. Many magnetizers keep somnambulists in that state after their cure, hoping to use them to provide service to other patients; but it is wrong to place confidence in such somnambulists. They are often used for experiments of curiosity. They are exhibited to people who question them on various subjects. None of this does any good. It does not even convince the skeptics, and it presents many inconveniences.

### *Third—Of the Dangers to which People expose themselves who place too much Confidence in Somnambulists.*

Many enthusiastic magnetizers have a blind faith in their somnambulists. They believe them to be infallible, both in the judgment they give of their own disease and in the diagnosis they give of the diseases of others. If the remedies they order do not succeed, they assume it is because the prescriptions have not been followed with enough precision; if the remedies have caused harm, they regard the harm as a necessary crisis. Because they have sometimes witnessed inconceivable wonders, they have become credulous, and this credulity causes them to lose all caution. Even when a mishap occurs, they remain under the illusion.

There are, without doubt, some somnambulists endowed with such lucidity that, when they have been placed in communication with a sick person, they clearly explain the origin, the cause, and the nature of the disorder, and prescribe the most suitable remedies by indicating the effects they should produce and the crises which are to be expected. They predict a disease which will develop in several months and the precautions that ought to be taken when the first symptoms become noticeable. They even see the moral condition of the patient,

Ecstatic somnambulism is often exhibited without being induced by Magnetism. If it is dangerous to consult somnambulists upon the dogmas of religion, it is no less so to consult them upon political affairs. I have seen men, who were otherwise well-informed, become the dupes of their visions and their predictions. I cannot recommend too highly that you never permit them to enter into such a course.

## CHAPTER IX.

### *ON THE MEANS OF DEVELOPING OUR MAGNETIC FACULTIES AND DERIVING BENEFIT FROM THIS DEVELOPMENT.*

When Mesmer announced his discovery, he refused to reveal a secret of which he considered himself the sole possessor, unless he was granted a certain number of select students to whom he could explain his entire theory and, at the same time, teach them the method of its application. However, to let the world know how vast and important that theory was, and to establish the priority of his discovery (*pour prendre date*), he published its fundamental principles in twenty-seven propositions. He withheld the proofs of these and promised to provide their development and explain their consequences as soon as an agreement was reached and measures were taken—measures he judged proper to prevent the abuse of his principles and to stop others from stealing the glory of his discovery. These propositions were very obscure. Several of them seemed contrary to the accepted principles of physics. They have never been clearly explained, and yet the practice of <term>Magnetism</term> has been attended with the greatest success. This proves that they were not as important as their author believed; and that the effects which he produced, and those which his pupils

The twenty-seventh of Mesmer’s propositions begins in this way: “ *This doctrine will enable the physician to form a correct judgment regarding the level of each individual’s health.* ”

People have not reflected enough on this proposition, and they will search in vain through most works on Magnetism to discover how it allows the physician to determine the state of the sick.

Mesmer also said, in the thirteenth proposition: “ *Experiment has proved the existence of a subtle matter, which penetrates all bodies without apparently losing its activity.* ” This proposition has been left unexplained, as has the twenty-seventh.

Mesmer later spoke extensively about currents, though no explanation has been given regarding what he meant by the term. The phenomenon mentioned by Mesmer has been known to a great number of his scholars. It was particularly known to M. d’Eslon, who directed the attention of almost all those to whom he taught the practice of Magnetism toward this subject. This knowledge was common to several of the members of the Society at Strasburg; and yet, in the numerous memoirs which they have published, they have spoken of it only in a vague manner, as if it were something known to everyone through oral tradition, which it is therefore useless to explain. I have myself scarcely said anything upon this subject in my “*Critical History*,” because I did not well understand its nature, and—not being endowed with the faculty of perceiving the diseases of others within myself, and not having paid attention to the action of the currents—I could not speak of it from my own experience. I have since read some manuscripts of M. d’Eslon in which the question has been treated; I have also read a manuscript work, written thirty-six years ago by a highly intelligent gentleman and excellent observer who, having first been instructed by M. d’Eslon, had added much to the knowledge he had acquired as a pupil; and I am convinced that what I had neglected to look into was a very remarkable phenomenon, the observation of which is the most useful in the practice of Magnetism.

Of course, I cannot set forth all the principles here, nor provide their explanation. I must limit myself to informing the reader of the main phenomenon and the indications it provides us with to better succeed in the treatment of diseases.

It is well known that good somnambulists discover the location of the diseases of persons placed in communication with them, sometimes by experiencing sympathetic pains in the part of their body corresponding with that which is affected in the patient; sometimes by passing their hands over them and examining them with attention from head to foot. It is also well known that, without any instruction, they magnetize much better than they do when awake, and that they direct the magnetic fluid in the most suitable way.

This ability to perceive the location of diseases and the direction which we ought to give to the fluid does not belong exclusively to somnambulists; it is also developed in many magnetizers when they are attentive to the different sensations they experience, either while magnetizing various patients or while applying the action of Magnetism to any organ of a patient with whom they are in communication.

# CHAPTER X.

## *OF THE STUDIES BY WHICH A PERSON MAY PERFECT HIMSELF IN THE KNOWLEDGE OF MAGNETISM.*

Magnetism may be considered from two points of view—either as the mere employment of a faculty which God has given us, or as a science whose theory encompasses the greatest problems of physiology and psychology, and whose applications are extremely varied.

Therefore, it follows that the people who are engaged in this subject may be divided into two classes:

The first class includes those who, having recognized in themselves the faculty of doing good by Magnetism—or, at least, hoping to succeed in it—wish to make use of it in their families or among their friends, or with some poor patients, but who, having duties to fulfill or business to follow, do not magnetize except in circumstances where it appears necessary to them, without seeking publicity, without any motive other than charity, and without any other aim than that of curing or relieving suffering humanity.

The second class is composed of men who, having leisure, wish to combine the practice of Magnetism with the study of the phenomena it exhibits; to engage in it extensively; to establish treatments for taking care of many patients at a time; to train pupils capable of aiding them; and to have somnambulists who

In all sciences, we should begin with the simplest principles and progress, by degrees, to those that are complex. The solution to the most advanced problems in physics would be unintelligible to anyone who is ignorant of the laws of motion and the actions of electricity and caloric. It is the same in the study of this subject. You should begin by closely examining the simplest and most common effects—those which are produced daily with perfect ease and merely prove that Magnetism produces influences unique to itself—before you consider observing striking phenomena such as somnambulism; for these are complicated by several causes that must first be studied separately.

While reading published works on Magnetism, you should not neglect to become acquainted with those who practice it, in order to see, test, and collect new phenomena, and to distinguish what is common to all and what is unique to each of them. In the various phenomena that the same somnambulist often presents, you will strive to distinguish those that originate from the actions of the magnetizer from those that may have been produced or modified by the will or imagination of the patient; those caused by a heightened excitation of the sensory organs from those that signal the development of a unique sense; and finally, those that demonstrate a more or less extensive clairvoyance—displayed only regarding real and perceptible objects—from those where that same clairvoyance is clouded by illusions. After having collected a great number of phenomena, you should endeavor to classify and compare them, and to establish a theory resulting from this comparison, if, perhaps, we have arrived at the point where it would be truly philosophical to form a theory. Up to the present time, nearly all the writers who have wished to lay down general principles have founded them upon some facts of the same order, without regard to other facts to which they are not applicable. Hence, to discover general laws, it is necessary not only to have seen many facts with your own eyes, but to have collected a great number of others, which are to be carefully proven and all their circumstances scrutinized.

He should let the phenomena present and develop themselves, and note them down after each session.

The most difficult thing for a <term>magnetizer</term> who wishes to learn is that he must have within himself, as it were, two persons who must not exist at the same time, but successively: one to act, and the other to reason.

While you are magnetizing, you must occupy yourself entirely with the cure of the patient to whom you have devoted your time. You must not investigate; you must not take note of anything; you must withdraw from all prejudices, opinions, and knowledge; even reason itself should not be busy; the soul should have only one active faculty—the will to do good; the mind only one idea—confidence in success. <note>You must follow this rule not only when you are magnetizing yourself, but also when you are permitted to see phenomena. You must then unite your intentions with the magnetizer, and look on attentively without allowing yourself to form any judgment. In a word, you must conduct yourself when you assist at a magnetic session just as if you were carrying out the process yourself, with this single difference: when you are merely a witness, you must not exert your will except in subordination to that of the magnetizer.</note>

But after the end of the session, you will recall to your mind what you have seen; you will take note of it; you will combine all the circumstances, search for the causes, and try to reach results which will be more certain as subsequent observations confirm them. The magnetizer, while acting, should have unbounded confidence; he should doubt nothing. But when he takes note of the phenomena presented to him, he should be distrustful, doubtful of everything, and admit no fact except upon incontestable evidence—no principle, unless supported by a series of observations consistent with each other, and which are not contrary to any of the truths of physics and physiology.

<term>Magnetism</term>, considered as an agent, is entirely different from the other agents of nature. It has its own laws, which are not identical to the laws of matter. Considered as a science, it has peculiar principles that cannot be known except through observation; no idea of these can be grasped from known sciences. I can say this much with certainty; but I permit myself to add an opinion here—one shared by myself and many enlightened men—which I propose merely as an opinion:

The theory of <term>Magnetism</term> is based upon this great principle: that there are two sorts of elements in nature, radically different in their characteristics and properties—spirit and matter; and that these two elements act upon each other, though each possesses laws peculiar to itself. Among the laws that regulate the action of matter upon matter, many have been successively brought to light by observation, determined by calculation, and verified by experiment; such are the laws of motion, attraction, electricity, the transmission of light, and so on. It is not the same with the mind; although the existence of our soul has been demonstrated and many of its faculties are known to us, its nature remains a mystery, its union with organized matter is inconceivable, and most of the laws by which mind acts upon mind are unknown. # APPENDIX.
