->NOTE I.<-

*This work was originally published in three parts, and the appendix of each part included such communications as were received at the time of its publication. It was then intended to create a new arrangement of these and the translator’s notes as soon as another edition was sent to the press; however, on reflection, it seems better to preserve the original form and add the new notes at the end.*

*It must now be apparent to everyone familiar with <term>Mesmerism</term>, that many of the experiments detailed in this Appendix must have been harmful to their subjects. They can find no excuse except for the inexperience of those who permitted them, and in their strong desire to convince scientific men of the power of this agency, which had then been recently introduced to our notice. It is, however, useful to let them remain, since they tend to decrease public curiosity to see them repeated in proportion to the authenticity by which they are supported; and since they establish, through the most respectable testimony, the fact of the wonderful influence that may be exercised. We must look to that portion of the correspondence contributed by physicians of high standing for the legitimate use of this agency. In such hands, it is destined to produce much good as a supplement to medicine.*

Miss S—, in this city, was found to be asleep in the schoolroom about a month ago during an intermission. One of the young students came and reported it. Miss S— and others tried to wake her, but when they did not succeed, they became alarmed. A young medical student, a son of Commodore John Orde Creighton, was called in and soon perceived that she was in a magnetic sleep. A little girl, about ten years old, revealed her involvement in the matter by bursting into tears. She was so terrified by the result of the mischief that Miss S— called her into another room, calmed her distress, and told her she need not be frightened; she only had to go to Anne and ask her to wake up. This was done. She simply spoke to her, and she came out of her magnetic state with that smile on her face which is characteristic of those who are gently awakened from it.

The child had been put into the somnambulic state once before, and only once. It was achieved in about five minutes by a lady who had never before tried her *hand* at this practice.

I learned these details from Mr. Benjamin Cozzens and Mr. Joseph Balch, Jr.

An instance of the power of magnetizing without physical contact, and causing sleep on the *first* attempt, is provided by the case of a woman in a nervous state. She was put to sleep for the first time by her husband within fifteen minutes, without her knowing anything of his intention, while she sat in one part of the room and he in another. When she was asleep, he went into an adjoining room, out of her direct sight, and, taking down a book, began to read it. After being in the magnetic state for some time, she was awakened. She correctly described what he had done and showed the usual proofs of clairvoyance. The gentleman is a resident of this city and a friend of mine, whose truthfulness I can trust.

Dr. ——, of this city, informed me that one of his daughters, seven years of age, put her little sister, between two and three years of age, into a deep magnetic sleep, so that her mother could not wake her. Sometime afterward, the younger child was very eager to experience the effect again and cried because she was not permitted to be magnetized. See page 202.

### NOTE III.—Page 54.

The power exercised over the patient's imagination is one of the most remarkable things connected with this subject. The success of all experiments of this kind depends upon the control the magnetizer has over his own imagination, as well as upon its inherent strength. Long practice will enable a person to call up a clear mental image of the item he wishes to administer; and he will succeed in proportion to the clarity and strength of this conception, all else being equal.

While holding a glass of water in your hand, have the magnetizer called into another room, where a person you select will whisper to him what you want the water to taste like. The magnetizer returns, focuses his mind on the glass of water to give it the desired quality, and requests the somnambulist to take it from your hand and drink it. He will then ask the subject what he is drinking. The somnambulist rarely fails to identify it, if it is something with which he is familiar. It may be that he is only slightly familiar with the drink whose taste is being projected into the water; in this case, another condition is clearly required to make the trial satisfactory: namely, the patient must know the item being suggested to him.

An empty glass works as well as a full one. A peach may thus be transformed into an apple, a pear, an iron ball, and so on. A folded handkerchief may be changed into a child, a cat, or a dog, and placed in the patient's lap. In the first case, it will be fondled; in the second, it will be thrown off violently or caressed, depending on the person's feelings or prejudices.

Nor is it true, as some suppose, that the effect is produced merely upon the patient's imagination. Any medicine that the magnetizer can form a strong mental image of may be administered in this manner, and it will be accompanied by all its usual effects, just as if it were actually taken. This is a well-known and common fact.

### NOTE IV.—Page 102.

**CLAIRVOYANCE.**—This term is used to describe the faculty peculiar to somnambulists and people with epilepsy, which enables them to see things nearby and also distant things without appearing to use their eyes. It seems to be a more expressive word than any other in the English language that could be used to convey its meaning, because the idea intended to be conveyed is unique; we must either limit a familiar word to one of its meanings, invent a new one, or adopt the one already introduced, which is appropriate in the terminology of <term>Magnetism</term>. Its literal meaning is *clear-sightedness*; its technical meaning is *clear-sightedness in the somnambulic state*.

Somnambulists, when they wish to examine an object attentively, generally press it lightly against the <term>epigastrium</term>. The translator has seen one case where the seat of vision was on the back part of the head, and another where it was on one side of the head, near the organ designated by <term>Spurzheim</term> as <term>alimentiveness</term>. The objects examined, such as bank bills and the addresses on letters, are always held with the blank side next to the seat of vision, so as to be read from right to left.

### NOTE V.—Page 219.

Among the somnambulists I have seen, a peculiar delicacy has been exhibited while in the magnetic state. Although the magnetizer undoubtedly possesses the power to change the appearance of things to their perception—such as turning an apple into a walnut or water into lemonade—he probably cannot destroy that natural sense of propriety which seems to be heightened in the somnambulist.

Foissac says, on page 392, that “when M. de Puységur saw, in 1784, the control which he exercised over somnambulists, he was alarmed at the thought that others might turn aside this power from its holy intention. But all his patients declared to him that they preserved in that state their judgment and their reason; that they perceived very quickly the designs of the magnetizer, and that these could easily cause them to awake. The authors I have cited in the preceding paragraph are of the same opinion. My somnambulists have told me exactly the same things. If, then, some instances of a contrary nature are brought against us, I will say that Magnetism has been the *pretext*, and not the *cause*, of these disorders; because it does not take from all those who practice it the vicious propensities of their hearts, and all the abuses of which complaint is made would have existed as much without it as with it.”

->NOTE VI.—Page 95.<-

The gentlemen who have practiced Magnetism in this country have arrived at the observation of the same general rules which govern the more experienced practitioners of Europe. This is the more remarkable, since they have been obliged to depend upon the experience which they gained from their own practice, due to a lack of proper means of information. This fact, about the consequences of making short passes before the head, which M. Deleuze calls charging it too much, was observed to me by one of them who had never read on the subject.

->NOTE VII.—Page 66-122.<-

It is not to be wondered at, then, if some rough attempts made to rouse a somnambulist, by persons who doubted the reality of the sleep, have achieved their goal and thrown a temporary suspicion upon Mesmerism itself, as though it professed to do what it could not perform. One instance of this kind has sometimes produced strong skepticism in the minds of many persons. Hence it is proper to know that there is always a liability, though a very slender probability,

Unfortunately, these curious phenomena must be displayed before Magnetism can gain converts who believe in its curative and restorative virtues; and few are satisfied with merely hearing about the power somnambulists possess to visit the houses of their neighbors and friends in spirit; everyone claims the privilege of sending one into their own house and hearing their own furniture described. They want the proof of Didymus; and when they have obtained it, they depart in wonder and astonishment, like the woman of Samaria from the well of Sychar, and relate what they have seen to excite the wonder and astonishment of others. Hence, those who merely hear of these phenomena form an estimate of the subject based not on its real utility, but on its curious nature. And there is some danger that its curative and restorative powers will be overlooked in the craze of curiosity. When this craze has subsided, the magnetizers will have the leisure to pursue their calling without interruption. *And the maxims of the benevolent Deleuze, who forbids such experiments, will command the respect and the attention which they deserve.*

### NOTE VIII.—Page 121.

#### PARALYSIS.

The translator himself has witnessed the exertion of this paralyzing power, both upon patients who were in a magnetic sleep and upon others who were not. However, he has not seen a person paralyze the limbs of another who had never been put into a magnetic sleep by him. It seems to be a necessary condition that perfect communication must have been established at some previous time. The power gained by the practice of Magnetism is so great, however, that it may be found effective in a trial of this kind even without this condition.

Among the persons who have possessed this extraordinary power, Gassner deserves special mention. A brief notice of him may be found in the volume by Doctor Foissac, page 446. I will translate a portion of it:

> "John Joseph Gassner, born at Braz in the Circle of Swabia in 1727, having been delivered through exorcism from a long-term illness which had resisted all the resources of medical art, convinced himself that the majority of human infirmities could be attributed to no other cause than demonic possession, and that they should be treated with exorcism. He began by curing the sick people of his own parish; but very soon Switzerland, Tyrol, and Swabia sent him theirs, and he cured four or five hundred a year. After having traveled through different provinces, he established himself at Ratisbon under the protection of the Prince-Bishop (*prince-évêque*). The number of persons resorting to him was so large that he often had ten thousand of them encamped in the neighborhood of Ratisbon. Gassner considered faith an essential condition for being cured. It was rare for patients to be freed from their afflictions during the first exorcism. He dedicated several hours, and often many days, to them. When he wished to act upon a patient, he made him kneel before him; he almost always touched the affected part. Sometimes he rubbed his hands upon his waist or upon his neck, but this was not always the case.
> 
> "Gassner had the power, by his will, to make the pulse of his patients vary; he made it small, large, strong, weak, slow, fast, irregular, or intermittent—ultimately, exactly as the physicians who were present requested of him. *He paralyzed their limbs*; caused them to weep or laugh; and soothed or agitated them simply by expressing his command in Latin, or rather, mentally.
> 
> "He thus performed the most extraordinary cures. Only a small number of people were found to contradict the facts."

> ‘Another description of phenomena, which may be called those of intelligence, is manifested in the <term>somnambulist</term>’s understanding the will of the <term>magnetizer</term>, or of the person with whom she may be in communication. To test this power, I have conducted a great number of experiments, which have been almost uniformly successful. She can, for instance, be willed to have in her hand various kinds of fruits, cakes, wines, animals, birds, etc.; or any other things may be changed from one to another at the will of the <term>magnetizer</term>.

> ‘There is a class of phenomena which seem to partake more of a physical character than those mentioned above, as witnessed in the attraction which takes place between the hand of the <term>magnetizer</term> and the magnetized person, and also as witnessed in the attraction and repulsion in the application of the <term>artificial magnet</term>. I do not wish to be understood to mean that this phenomenon certainly partakes of a physical character, though the sudden, powerful, and apparently involuntary action of the <term>muscles</term> seems to favor this opinion. On the contrary, it must be admitted that the patient, in this case, not only understands the will of the <term>magnetizer</term>, but observes all his actions; and therefore these motions may be voluntary and in obedience to his will. Or, in using the magnet, a powerful influence may be produced upon the imagination, and those effects may be occasioned by the imagination acting upon an excitable <term>nervous system</term>.
> 
> ‘The lack of time and opportunity on my own part, and the desire to have as many distinguished and scientific persons see and investigate this case in their own way as has been consistent with her convenience, have prevented my making experiments calculated to establish this point conclusively; neither have I, for the same reasons, been able to determine, satisfactorily, whether all the senses can be used in reference to things not present, as is the case with vision.

### NOTE XI.

The following paper was prepared by M. B. L——, a gentleman at the head of one of our finest literary institutions, from notes taken at the time of the experiments. One thing adds much to its value, and that is the early date at which it *was written*. This also serves to explain why circumstances are stated so minutely, which are now so well known to accompany most experiments of this kind. There is no danger of being too detailed regarding this subject, since those who are familiar with its phenomena, and those who are not, are equally prone to form hasty conclusions without sufficiently considering the wide variety of phases they present and the complexity of principles they may involve. To create theories is very easy, but to observe facts requires patience and caution. Hence we hear men, every day, speaking dogmatically regarding this subject, as though they had established everything they utter through a careful observation of the facts as they exist; whereas its acknowledged difficulties ought to make us more cautious and more willing to dedicate care to it. This paper was not intended for publication:

himself, has been written. It contains a simple statement of certain phenomena produced by one individual upon another, principally through the power of the *will*, assisted by certain manipulations known as <term>*passes*</term>. The writer's attention was first called to the subject by reading notices published in Boston papers of wonderful effects caused by Bugard and others, such as producing a sleep so deep that a tooth could be—and actually was—pulled without causing any painful sensation. Far from trusting these statements, he thought little of the subject until an intimate friend gave him an account of a lecture he had attended (perhaps the previous evening) on *Animal Magnetism* by Charles Poyen. He was unscientific enough to exclaim, "I do not believe it!" and to attempt to prove its falsehood by its strangeness. This circumstance is mentioned to show that the writer was far from being prejudiced in favor of what was then generally believed to be a hoax.

> "As, however, it became the general topic of conversation, and as questions of this sort—'What do you think, Mr. ——, of *Animal Magnetism?*' 'Do you think, M——, there is anything in *Animal Magnetism?*' were repeatedly asked, to which, of course, he could give no satisfactory answer, he decided to take every opportunity to gain information which could help him form a judgment. Far from finding a partner in his immediate circle, he undertook the investigation alone.

> "To carry out this resolution, he attended Charles Poyen's lectures, witnessed his experiments at Pawtucket, and finally read the *Report of the French Commissioners*. (It is proper to remark that the experiments at Pawtucket were far from being satisfactory. It seemed to be the experimenter's opinion that the people came more to behold wonders than to investigate. There was apparently, therefore, no effort to remove whatever might lead to suspicion of trickery.) But still being unsatisfied, the only remaining way seemed to be for the writer to experiment for himself, which he did as follows.

The magnetizer then withdrew his hand and brought his head near to the forehead of the magnetized person, at which he showed the same uneasiness as at the south pole of the magnet. The novel thought occurred to the magnetizer that perhaps he himself might be magnetized negatively by induction. He therefore decided to form a circuit and learn the result. It was formed by placing the hand of the magnetizer upon the head of the magnetized person, and the hand of the magnetized person upon the head of the magnetizer. Just as the connection was being made, the magnetized person sprang as if he had received an electric shock, though nothing was felt by the magnetizer. I— H— tried the same, with the same result.

But it was in vain; the shocks were felt as before. Glass proved *not* to be a non-conductor. On being awakened, he had no recollection of what had occurred, but complained that he felt as if he had been receiving severe electric shocks.

magnetizer is a strong objection to his own conclusion,

### NOTE XIII.
#### *SOMNAMBULISM.*

No one who reads medical works is unaware of the frequent occurrence of natural somnambulism. A hundred cases could undoubtedly be quoted from the best authorities. A remarkable and well-authenticated case recently appeared in the *Boston Medical and Surgical Journal*. I do not know whether to classify the following story, which I found in a very old translation of Pliny’s *Natural History*, as fact or fiction. Does its resemblance to what is known to take place in induced somnambulism not authorize us to consider it as having *some* foundation in truth?

> "We read in the Chronicles that the spirit of Hermotimus of Clazomenae was accustomed to abandon his body for a time. Wandering through far-off countries, he used to bring home news from remote places about things that could not possibly be known unless he had been present there. All the while, his body lay as if half dead in a trance. He continued this practice so long that at last the Cantharidae, who were his mortal enemies, took his body and burned it to ashes. By that means, they deprived his poor soul, when it returned, of that sheath or case, so to speak, where it intended to reside."—*Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 52.*

There is some similarity between the story above and the following one, which is extracted from Watson’s *Annals of Philadelphia*, page 235, 1830 edition.

The Marquis de Puységur says, in his work entitled "*Recherches Physiologiques sur l'Homme*" <note>*Physiological Research on Man*</note>, page 423: "There are <term>somnambulists</term> whose active energy makes them almost spontaneously perceive all that can be useful and beneficial to themselves. There are also some who are inert and lazy, whose intuitive faculties are not manifested unless their development is aided. A <term>somnambulist</term> may be compared to a person with very good eyes who is unexpectedly placed upon a height rising from a vast plain. His vision would sweep over a great area without distinguishing anything. He would wonder at all things without noticing any; and the most beautiful situations, the most interesting objects, would often be the very ones to which he would pay no attention. It is exactly the same with many <term>somnambulists</term>. If you do not stop and fix their attention upon what ought particularly to interest them, they will often observe nothing in the vast and indefinite domain of their perception."

## NOTE XIV.

### *TRAVELLING SOMNAMBULISTS.*

The <term>somnambulist</term> always appears to have a perfect knowledge of what the <term>magnetizer</term> is doing. If he occasionally loses track of him, it is because some other person is in communication and absorbs his whole attention. But the <term>magnetizer</term> generally keeps his control over his patient, even though at a distance from him; that is, he can cause him to sink into a state of insensibility; he can make him answer the question of one person and return no answer to the question of another; he can make him lose the power of seeing anyone present; he can make him call for any particular article of food, or wake him suddenly, etc.—all by the mere power of the will. It sometimes happens that such experiments fail, but it is evident that the patient commonly has the faculty of sensing the *will* of his <term>magnetizer</term>. He seems to be drawn toward him by an intense impulse. He can almost always tell where he is. I have known one <term>somnambulist</term> who,

<term>Somnambulists</term> frequently enter the wrong house and often give a wrong description when they enter the right house; and it requires some skill to get them to correct the errors they fall into at first sight, as well as to discover the cause of their making such errors.

But when they enter a house, or imagine they have entered one—which neither they nor anyone present has ever been inside—they will give a description that is consistent within itself, whether it is true or false regarding the house they are supposed to be visiting. Thus, if the <term>somnambulist</term> describes the fireplace in the parlor as being on the north side, and a door on the right of the fireplace leading into the room behind the parlor, he will, when taken into that back room, make the fireplace there correspond with the position of the chimney previously indicated in the description of the first room. As soon as I noticed this consistency, I varied the experiments significantly to determine if it is always so. After examining one room in a house in relation to the position of the windows and the grates, I proceeded to a back room on the second or third story to get a description of it; then down into the yard to get a description of the back part of the house; then into the front yard to look into the parlor window and describe the situation of things from this new point of view; then to one side of the house to look in at a window into a room in which we had not yet been; then into a room on the second story, directly above the room behind the parlor, and the fireplace was found to be on the south side, exactly corresponding

### NOTE XVI.

When a <term>somnambulist</term> has anything in his hand, the <term>magnetizer</term> may will him to give it to any person in the room, and it will be done accordingly, even though not a word is said by anyone. If another individual attempts to take it by grasping it, or by sliding his hand between the object and the hand of the person to whom it is offered, the <term>somnambulist</term> evades him with the speed of thought and places it where he was requested to place it. I have seen several persons try in this manner, all at the same time, to seize the object, but without success. With almost inconceivable dexterity of evasion, the <term>somnambulists</term> maintained their own hold and delivered the item safely.

What is equally remarkable was related to me by Mr. Potter. A patient of his, with whom I am acquainted, has no *sight*—that is, she has no <term>clairvoyance</term>—when she is in the <term>somnambulic</term> state. Yet, when requested to hand any object to another person, she will not give it up to anyone but the designated individual, even though the <term>magnetizer</term> tries to exert no influence at the time. She does not offer any explanation for this herself, but says she always knows when the right person presents his hand, even when he says nothing. This has been witnessed by several of my friends. ### NOTE XVII.

Somnambulists frequently display striking ingenuity and sharpness of thought. An example can be given that was told to me by Dr. Cleveland of Pawtuxet.

Professor Yates of Schenectady and the Reverend Mr. Dumont of Newport had been invited by him to see one of his patients while she was in a somnambulic state. After various experiments to test the lady's clairvoyance, one of the gentlemen—perhaps to clear away any remaining doubts—opened the New Testament and, pointing to a verse, asked her to read it. She refused to read it at first, but finally said she would read a verse on the opposite page. When asked to do so, she pointed her finger to the following passage and read it: "*Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe!*"—John 4:48.

### NOTE XVIII.

The following passage is taken from one of Lafayette’s letters to Washington. Since it was written in English, the reader will notice the peculiarities that mark it as the work of a foreigner. It is found in the "*Memoirs, Correspondence, and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, published by his Family*," in three volumes, recently published by Messrs. Saunders & Otley of New York.

> "A German doctor named Mesmer, having made the greatest discovery regarding *Animal Magnetism*, has instructed students, among whom your humble servant is considered one of the most enthusiastic. I know as much as any magician ever did, which reminds me of our friend's interview with the devil at Fishkill that made us laugh so much at his house. Before I leave, I will get permission to let you in on Mesmer's secret, which, you can be certain, is a grand philosophical discovery."

superstition, at least in some of its forms. The superstitious are those who, through ignorance, attribute natural appearances and events to supernatural causes, and they are the least likely to have faith in the power of this agent. Biased as they generally are by the opinion that supernatural influence is exerted in all uncommon things which they cannot explain, they are unwilling to listen to anyone who refers them to a principle whose laws are hardly known. They see all history full of inexplicable stories, and they view the attempt to explain them rationally as daring, and even impious. Such is the case with some very conscientious but very weak-minded people. They do not consider that Omnipotence is displayed as much in the extraordinary application of known principles as in the application of those which are hidden from us, and that the idea of a violation of natural laws does not necessarily enter into the meaning of the word *miracle*. The word *miraculous*, meaning *wonderful*, may with appropriateness be applied to every exertion of Divine power which surpasses our ordinary experience. But if it were necessary to quiet the fears of such people, it might be stated that even the smallest miracle recorded in Holy Scripture is beyond comparison greater than anything accomplished by this agent. The turning of water into wine and the healing of the sick by touch are the only things that are even slightly resembled by magnetic action. To claim that the two things are the same is an assumption not supported by a careful attention to the facts. And if, in these two cases, the same agent is employed, we cannot help but notice a vast difference in the effects produced. In one, the cure is instantaneous; in the other, it is long and tedious. In the one, there is no failure; in the other, there is uncertainty.

The tree that is made to spring from the earth instantaneously to a great size, and the one that grows its branches one by one, reaching maturity in a hundred years, may both be sustained by the same laws of vegetative growth, accelerated in one case and not in the other. Yet the first displays an instance of miraculous power exerted, and the other follows the course of nature in its slow development. It is not, therefore, a detraction from the virtue of recorded

miracles to *suppose* we have obtained a faint glimpse of the principles by which they were performed; but the supposition is unfounded.

The crude and ill-digested state of our knowledge on this subject, the wonderful effects which have been produced, and the suggestive energy with which they are filled, have led enthusiastic men into a wide and boundless field of speculation. They imagine there are no limits to this power, because they cannot determine them.

They are like the first discoverers of Nootka Sound, who recorded it on their charts as a vast inland sea, simply because the mist prevented them from seeing the opposite shore. They do mischief to the cause of truth by rash attempts to sustain unfounded theories; and they are the ones who have introduced the doctrine to which reference has been made.

When we examine the subject calmly, we shall find in it traces of what has been practiced for centuries. Witchcraft, magic, exorcism, and sorcery will soon no longer be capable of perplexing the minds of men; for superstition will be known no more. As the progress of astronomy dispelled the dread inspired by eclipses and by comets, which "from their horrid hair shook pestilence and war," so may the discovery of this new power in the human mind destroy the lingering remnants of superstition, while it also rescues from the reproach of utter falsehood many a tale of barbaric times.

### NOTE XX.—Page 145.

**TRANSMISSION OF PAIN.**—The transmission of symptoms from the magnetizer to the magnetized is frequent, and it is for this reason that Deleuze considers good health indispensable in a magnetizer. In the case of Madame Montaux, we see the opposite effect taking place. If this occurs more frequently than we are aware of, it may account for the peculiar oppression and weakness which some persons feel after magnetizing. And if there be any truth in the theory of a fluid, the directions given by Deleuze to flick the fingers at the end of a pass, in order to throw it off from ourselves, derive additional weight from this circumstance, and are worthy of being implicitly followed in cases of contagious disease.

I have known a somnambulist, while in her natural state, to be afflicted with a violent side ache as a result of sitting down and taking the hand of a patient who was then being magnetized for that ailment. Her susceptibility to magnetic influence was so great that, although the magnetizer did not direct his attention to her, she was the first of the two to fall into the magnetic state.

The same thing has been observed by the celebrated physiologist *Georget*. He says that whenever he put his somnambulists in communication with a sick person, they immediately experienced pain, uneasiness, and sometimes a sharp ailment in the corresponding organs.

->NOTE XXI.—Page 159.<-

**THE MAGNETIC FLUID.**—I have heard patients say they can see the magnetic fluid, just as M. N.’s patients did. Whether this is an illusion of the imagination, or whether a fluid actually exists, has long been a question among scholars. M. Bertrand, in his work on somnambulism, rejects the belief in its existence. He says that the idea originates or is perpetuated in the minds of the magnetizers and is then transferred into the minds of their patients. There is little doubt that this might be the case if there were no fluid; however, it has frequently happened that patients have claimed to see the fluid even when those who magnetized them were not *fluidists*. And it must also be remembered that the imagination of somnambulists cannot be permanently affected regarding an object. As soon as the operator’s will ceases to act, the object returns to what it really is. For instance, he may cause a lady's workbag to take on the appearance of a child, and he may induce the patient to caress it as such; but the moment he withdraws his attention from the subject, it returns to its proper appearance and she hugs the illusion no longer.* If you try this experiment and find that every impression of that kind is necessarily temporary, will there not be some

Is there not a difficulty in adopting Bertrand's notion? Besides, it requires a *positive effort* to create a deception of any kind, and many who try to do so fail because they have not exerted enough mental energy. It would therefore seem impossible for a *simple opinion* among magnetizers that such a fluid exists to produce an illusion so strong as to deceive their somnambulists and make them constantly state the same thing regarding its existence.

It should, however, be kept in mind that since somnambulism presents such a great variety of phases and is accompanied by such a diversity of powers, we cannot be too cautious in adopting theories—especially those that tend to prevent all further investigation of the points in question.

It should be stated here that some somnambulists do not see any fluid, even when their attention is directed to it.

If anyone thinks this is a strong objection to the theory of a fluid, let them remember that somnambulists vary greatly in their power of clairvoyance; and not only that, but the same individual has it very weak at one time and very strong at another. It is difficult to conceive how any effect can take place without a material medium. It may be granted that somnambulism *might*, under certain circumstances, occur by the mere power of the imagination, but this does not by any means allow for the conclusion that the *phenomena* are attributable to the same cause, or that the will and influence of another's mind do not produce any effect when they are exerted. Polarity may be given to an iron rod, heated to a certain degree and held in a certain direction, by a sharp blow at one end with a hammer; and the rod may acquire polarity by the silent operation of nature over a long period of time if left in the same position. But if, from the latter fact, we infer that the hammer had no role in the former instance, we are guilty of an absurdity entirely similar to the one suggested above.

Assuming, then, that the effect is produced by the <term>vis voluntatis</term> <note>the power of the will</note> of the magnetizer, and that it is difficult to conceive how it can act without a medium, we should not reject an opinion supported by the authority of perhaps nine-tenths of the European writers on the subject, unless we can offer the justification of a thorough investigation...

But we could give another reason in favor of the theory. The passes are always made downwards to produce an effect, and upwards or transversely when we wish to lessen the magnetic action or relieve it entirely.

Let anyone try one instead of the other, and the result may assist him in perceiving the force of the argument. If a patient requires the manipulations in order to be put to sleep, and you cannot effect it by the upward passes, is it not proof that the imagination does not play the most important part in producing the magnetic sleep? Of course, it must not be forgotten that some magnetizers make no passes at all with very susceptible persons; but since the passes are generally requisite, we may argue from the general fact.

**BLINDNESS.**—In the appendix to the first part of this work, I have inserted some articles in relation to Miss Loraina Brackett, which the reader will remember. ### NOTE XXV.

The reader is presented here with letters from various physicians, which cannot fail to be highly interesting—not only because of the nature of the cases whose treatment is described, but because of the high reputation of the authors within their own profession. Most of the intelligent physicians in the country are turning their attention to this subject, desiring to become acquainted with its claims as a healing agent; and, so far, it has proved itself to the satisfaction of everyone who has approached it in this spirit. These letters embrace exactly such cases as are stated in Deleuze, and have thus validated the “Practical Instruction” with evidence of its inherent value.

### *CORRECTION OF THE HABITS OF SOMNAMBULISTS.*

The influence which the magnetizer—with the consent of the somnambulist—is able to exert upon their waking state through their somnambulism may be easily proved by various experiments of simple curiosity; however, the magnetizer should rarely indulge in this kind of experimentation. This power may, however, frequently be rendered highly useful in the correction of habits—not only physical ones, but mental ones as well. The following instances where the writer has, with some success, employed this influence for the benefit of his patients, may serve as illustrations of this power, and may encourage magnetizers to resort to its use in all similar cases.

One individual, of a highly nervous temperament and greatly affected by dyspepsia, had at times an almost irresistible craving for certain fruits and foods, which were sure to upset her stomach and worsen her nervous symptoms.

Having, upon my first attempt at Magnetism, very easily induced somnambulism, I resolved to test this power—though with little confidence in the success of the attempt, as it had previously been impossible to restrain the patient in her use of certain items. I accordingly instructed her, in the most impressive manner, not to indulge in their use. The following day, having obtained an apple, she wished to eat it, but found herself under the control of a mysterious influence which made it morally impossible. It seemed to her that a person told her, while she was asleep, not to eat such things. “And,” she said, “I do not think I shall be able to eat one all summer.”

I soon found that I had not included one important item in my prohibition, namely, tea—which she had freely indulged in for years. I believed it exerted such an unfavorable influence upon her nerves that I had for a long time used every means to persuade her to abandon it, but without success. I therefore issued the order; and, as every law usually has its appropriate penalty, I added one as follows: that the use of even the smallest quantity should be followed by nausea. The experiment was perfectly successful, as all subsequent attempts to take tea were followed by distressing sickness. As long as she remained in the family where she was then staying, she continued to be unable to take either tea or the forbidden articles of food. I was informed two months later that those habits remained corrected, and it is to be hoped that they are permanently cured.

I had observed another somnambulist who had the habit of taking air into the stomach while swallowing. Suspecting that the practice tended to increase the distress she sometimes experienced in her stomach, I directed her to swallow no more air—or, if she did so, that she should be seized with a pain in the throat. This pain was actually observed by the members of the family where she was boarding to seize her twice the following day. She later informed me, during somnambulism, that she believed she was being cured of the habit.

A third patient had long indulged freely in the use of tea and coffee, and they had become, as she supposed, absolutely

A similar course was subsequently pursued regarding snuff. She had long been in the habit of using this article in considerable quantities. She agreed, but for some time after waking, she continued its use as before. At length, after taking a pinch, the sudden contortions of her face and her strong exclamations of loathing and disgust plainly indicated what had occurred. She had unwittingly exceeded her limits; she had taken the prohibited pinch and could take no more during the day. The following day, she could take it; but her craving for it daily diminished, as she was several times dreadfully annoyed by the seventh pinch. The habit was thus entirely broken, and only a tiny amount in comparison has been used in several months. She attributed the effect to the constant use of magnetized water.

From the following example, we are led to suppose that certain habits and weaknesses, especially mental ones, might be corrected by the same means, which, unfortunately, are applicable only to somnambulists. She told me, while in her somnambulism, that she had tried very hard to overcome this weakness—which was a source of much embarrassment and inconvenience to her—but without success, and she begged me to help her. I therefore followed the same course in this instance as I had before. Now apparently assured in her own mind that her failing was cured, she thanked me in the most grateful terms; and, although she was totally unaware while awake of what had occurred during her somnambulism, she assisted at the next preparation for a funeral without any sign of her former weakness.

These facts, like others pertaining to Animal Magnetism, will undoubtedly seem very extraordinary and will not be believed by those who have not examined the subject in the true spirit of philosophical investigation; however, they are confirmed by many writers on the subject. A work entitled “Cures Effected in France by Animal Magnetism” details various similar facts. To those who wish to put this science to use, these facts may provide hints that could lead to highly useful results. The writer would be pleased to show the evidence of these or any other interesting facts in his possession to those who wish to candidly investigate the subject.

### NOTE XXVIII.—Page 102.

**DISTANT CLAIRVOYANCE.**—The following letters are inserted for the purpose of satisfying a rational curiosity regarding the travels of the spirit during somnambulism. Others will appear in the third part. They are from gentlemen who are well known in this region, and their authority is second to none that can be produced. The reflecting mind will find in them enough to excite activity of thought, and even those most focused on the senses will find enough to be kindled into a spiritual flame, though it may flicker and be temporary in its rising. That the human spirit has the power to leave the body and perceive things distant in space is but an elementary truth in this branch of psychology. He who cannot grasp the evidence on which it rests with a firm hold will find himself constantly vacillating between belief and instability of faith; but he who has once weighed it, and allowed the conviction to produce its legitimate effect, will find his notions of things to come quickened and informed, and will be happy in the consciousness of immortality. For, if we are convinced that the spirit can be absent, or partially absent, from the body, and, while deriving little or no sensation from it, be engaged in real scenes in other climates, we are provided with the nourishment which strengthens our conceptions of a separate spiritual existence, so that the doctrine of a future state appears to be a consequence of our nature, if not susceptible to direct proof.

On asking her who she saw in the room below, she described three individuals, two of whom she recognized as having seen the day before, and the other as an elderly Quaker lady, whose very peculiar dress she described with the greatest accuracy and with considerable humor. This was the end of my experiment, as the time fixed by Dr. Capron for her to wake up was near at hand; and I hastened to lead her back to Providence. I arrived at the end of my imaginary journey just as the time expired, at which moment she awoke. On my return home, I confirmed that all her descriptions relating to the members of my family were perfectly correct.

"At the time of our supposed visit, my daughter *was alone* in the house—with the exception of the children, who were in bed—and sitting in the room where she was described to be. The other three members of the family *did return* about the time at which our experiments concluded, and were in the lower room, as described by Miss Brackett. Furthermore, Mrs. F., on visiting the little boy on her return, found him in precisely the uncomfortable situation which so much distressed the sympathetic invisible visitor.

"You will excuse me from making any observations or offering any opinion upon these remarkable phenomena. As facts, you are perfectly welcome to them, and to make what use of them you please; I am satisfied that all remarkable facts, but particularly those of a character not referable to any known principle, should be made public.

"Yours truly,
"E. L. FROTHINGHAM.
"Mr. T. C. HARTSHORN."

### FROM REVEREND E. B. HALL.

“To Mr. T. C. HARTSHORN: “PROVIDENCE, December 1, 1837.
“DEAR SIR: You wish me to write you something about my experience and opinions on the subject of Animal Magnetism. I have been unwilling to say anything publicly about that of which I know so little; and I should decline now, if my name had not already appeared in several journals without my permission, and in support of facts not correctly given. It was so in the reference to me which the appendix to your first number contained, afterwards quoted by Colonel Stone, although there was no exaggeration. A man’s own opinion may be of little importance; but truth is of great importance on all subjects, and especially as to matters of observation and fact. I feel willing, therefore, and feel it to be due to others, to say, in brief, what I have seen and what I believe.
“I can do this best by giving a view, first, of the principles by which, not I alone, but many observers in this city, have examined this subject, and then of some of the results, so far as they can be called results. There seems to be an impression abroad, and here also, with many, that those of us who have not had sufficient confidence in our own wisdom, nor seen sufficient cause in the facts offered, to pronounce this whole affair a fraud, or reject it as an absurdity, are entirely believers and dupes. How far we are dupes, I am not concerned to say. That we are not believers, I do say. I believe I may say it of a very large portion of the intelligent people in this place, though I am not authorized to speak for others. What is exactly intended, in saying that we are not believers, will appear from what follows. It may not be useless, to this or any cause, to speak of principles of evidence—the kind of inquiry and test to which all matters of this kind should be subjected—and the distinction between inquiring and believing. “The reality of what is called <term>Animal Magnetism</term> is purely a question of *fact*. I view it as such; it is only as a fact that I attach any importance to what is said or done about it. Whether it is new or old; whether it agrees with preconceived opinions or opposes them all; whether the wise men in France from the last century, or those of the present, believe or disbelieve; whether the marvelous powers supposed here, if real, would do most good or evil; whether the ‘possessed nuns,’ the ‘Salem witches,’ and the ‘old wives’ of all ages and both sexes have not performed as great wonders as modern <term>somnambulists</term>—these are all questions of lively interest, it is true, and proper for inquiry, but they are utterly ineffective, if not irrelevant, in settling a question of fact. Regarding fears or hopes about the truth of <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, I have neither. I do not have the least concern whether it proves to be true or false. I know it *is* either true or false, whether it is proven so or not, and whether I, or any man, or all men, believe or reject it. If it is false, it will do no great harm. If it is true, it will do good; for all truth is good and does good. Its interference with any other truth is impossible. It is not in the power of <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, or anything else, known or unknown, to destroy one particle of truth in religion, nature, or humanity. TRUTHS are never destroyed. They are not from man; he can neither create nor destroy the smallest of them. They are from God, and they are imperishable. There is but one question and one investigation, in this or any subject, that should cause great anxiety or be deemed essential—*What is truth?*

“Now, in seeking the truth regarding <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, it seems to me there has been too much credulity—too easy a faith—among many. incredulous. A healthy mind will never—as it cannot—believe that which is wholly strange, intrinsically improbable, and not yet supported by evidence suited to its nature or proportioned to its magnitude. And much of the evidence offered in this case, and relied upon, is neither of the kind nor degree that the case demands. I have seen many trials where the truth of everything was almost taken for granted, and the men and women merely looked on with open mouths. Supposing the ‘subject’ was, of course, asleep and insensible to all sounds and sights, they have openly said and done everything, and then wondered that she knew it! This is extraordinary folly. It is child’s play. The true principle in testing such supposed wonders is to take nothing for granted; no, nothing. I attend the examinations without assuming a single fact in the case, but rather doubting everything until it is proved. The whole matter is improbable—*i. e.*, it is opposed by all we have ever seen and all we know. I have a right, therefore, to institute the most rigid and suspicious scrutiny on every point. I will not believe simply because the operator is an honest man and the subject is pure and true. I do not dispute that, and it is to be taken into account. But it does not of itself prove much in a case like this. The best men in the world may be deceived, and so may the wisest. Indeed, such is human nature that, in certain circumstances, the best and wisest may deceive others, however unintentionally. I will not believe even my own senses in matters so unaccountable until I have had frequent opportunities of examining them. I hold that anything which is possible is more probable than that a person should see without eyes and travel without moving. I demand, therefore, for such facts, such evidence as it is not possible to evade or resist. So long as there can be any evasion or other explanation, my own mind will not receive the appearances as facts, whether others receive them or not, and whether I wish to receive them or not.

I distrust all information given when that information could have been obtained either from hints carelessly dropped in the room, or from personal interaction and previous knowledge of objects and places. To prove a case of actual *clairvoyance* or of mental locomotion, there must be not only no probability, but no possibility of any of the aforementioned aids or explanations. Nor can I conceive of more than one kind of proof for this particular power, which is so inconceivable and inexplicable. That proof is the awareness of holding in one’s mind a fact unknown to all others, proposing the inquiry ourselves in the most guarded manner, without any suggestion, hint, or help of any kind, and then hearing a true and unequivocal answer. It is of little value to hear others ask questions when you do not know what communication may have taken place previously. It is insufficient even to be told that letters were read through many bandages and envelopes if you know nothing of the participants, even if you believe their assertions. For letters have been read by specialized methods without being opened; and letters have been opened and returned so well-sealed that the writer himself could not detect any sign of change. Therefore, while I disclaim all suspicion of foul play in the cases of this kind occurring here, I insist that they are not positive proof of the power of seeing through opaque substances, except where the letter is never for a moment lost sight of by the writer or operator. If it is not lost sight of, but openly read and its contents correctly stated, then this is also evidence of the highest kind—supposing, as before, that the writer is sure no one but himself knows what the letter contains.

“These things are said, not for their specific value, but as an explanation of the kind of feelings and principles of evidence that many in this place have brought to this subject. They show that, so far at least, there has been no very great gullibility or tendency to be deceived. And I believe I may add—to speak now more specifically of the results—that, whether deceived or not, some of us have not been satisfied. If there are those who do not know the difference between inquirers and believers, or who think that the only wise ones are the scoffers, we must be excused from entering into any argument with them or about them. It violates all probability and all common sense to suppose that hundreds of men and women, of every profession and station, of unquestionable honesty and at least respectable information, without any coordination, payment, or identifiable motive, should engage in the same childish attempts at deception, produce the same strange results, and in different places become practitioners or subjects on a large scale, for no earthly reason but the pleasure of being fooled! 

Then, to crown the wisdom of such a supposition, it is only necessary to take a single case; for instance, that of a young woman of good sense and character faking total blindness for a year or two before she even hears of <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, in order to be prepared for it; subjecting herself to all manner of hardships; denying herself the pleasant privilege of seeing, working, eating, walking, or doing anything with comfort; falling repeatedly in this pretended blindness so as to receive serious injury and remain for weeks in severe pain and dangerous illness; then all at once managing, while her eyes are still closed and covered, to walk about easily and to see correctly; not for her own comfort or gain, but only for public entertainment or public suspicion; her family, physicians, and friends at home all the while asserting her actual blindness, and everyone with whom she lives being unable to detect in her a single sign of insincerity or even the power of manipulation; yet all of it a deception! Believe it who will. Find its parallel or explanation, if possible, in any case of witchcraft or delusion—or rather, deception; for it is important to distinguish them. Delusion there may be, of some kind, in this very case and every other; but deception there is not, if any evidence can be trusted or any fact proved by testimony or observation.

“This is the first result I have reached: namely, that there is no intentional deception in this matter. "A second conclusion to which I have come, in common with most inquirers, is in favor of the reality of the magnetic *sleep*. This follows, indeed, from a belief in the honesty of those concerned. But it deserves notice as a conviction that is almost universal now in the minds of those who have given any attention to the subject. There is no reason for the least doubt that a peculiar sleep is produced by certain manipulations, differing widely from common sleep, often accompanied by a suspension of sensibility, and sometimes by a remarkable activity of mind and power of communication. So far as this constitutes <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, I doubt if there are many informed minds, in this or any city, or any country, who doubt its reality.

"Of all beyond this, there are many who doubt, and there is reason for great modesty and caution. Then, too, there are so many failures made by every somnambulist, so many inequalities, inconsistencies, and perplexities, that it is wise, if not necessary, to suspend judgment and wait for greater revelations. It is true that inequalities and failures are no proof of the absence of the power. They belong to all states of mind and occur often even in the natural sciences. They count for something in favor of the honesty of the parties involved. And at all events, until we know what the power is, we have no right to prescribe laws or conditions—to say that it must always do this or never do that. We ought only to examine the matter more closely and extensively for this reason, and draw inferences and pronounce judgments with extreme caution.

“ ‘But they are facts,’ you say—‘what will you do with them?’ I can only say I do not know what to do with them. Facts they are, so far as I can discover. I have witnessed them, I have tried them severely, and I have been compelled to admit them in some cases. The evidence has sometimes, in a few instances of my own observation, been as high and complete as I can imagine. But the cases have not been sufficiently numerous and varied, nor the evidence sufficiently tested, to sustain belief in such extraordinary capacities. I will believe anything—or more properly, I must believe any and everything—that is proved, whether I understand its nature or not, and whether I can reconcile it with my preconceived notions or not. Its relations, its purpose, its uses, and its consequences, I leave with Him who gives all powers and ordains all truth. But it must be proved; and the proof must be proportional to the nature and magnitude of the thing to be established.

> “But, if not satisfied, I was confounded. *She described distant objects—whose position in some cases I had just changed, and whose existence in other cases I did not then know or believe—so truly and so wonderfully that I could only marvel. > “I regard the whole subject as a matter of curious study. It has no claim to be called a science, for that term implies something known and settled. It is hardly a subject for lectures or public speeches, much less for public displays and profit. It should be subjected to private and quiet examinations, scientific inquiry, and patient, rigid, unsparing experiment, yet conducted candidly and kindly. If it will not stand this trial, let it fail. If it will, let us learn what it is. I am told there is much being done now, privately and encouragingly. Yet it will not surprise me if the whole matter soon dies away and is not revived again for years. I am not optimistic about its progress or its benefits. If wisely pursued—neither blindly trusted nor blindly scorned—whatever truth or delusion it contains will appear in good time. As yet, I believe little, but hope for something, and fear nothing.

### FROM THE REV. MR. KENT.

->“ ROXBURY, November 27, 1837.<-

“ Mr. T. C. HARTSHORN:

“ DEAR SIR: I will give you a simple narrative of what happened in my presence on the evening when Miss Brackett was put into a <term>magnetic sleep</term> and conducted to my place of residence in Roxbury. I will describe the facts as they appeared to me, leaving you to use them as you think proper, and others to draw whatever conclusions from them they please. If I am accused of being too detailed, I will only say that my desire and purpose is to state the whole truth, without exaggeration or omission.

“ Intending to visit the Mansfield mines during my August vacation, I was persuaded by friends in Boston—who had recently witnessed the powers of various <term>somnambulists</term>—to go to Providence and seek an opportunity to see them myself. One of these friends kindly obtained for me the letter of introduction presented to you from your brother in Boston, in which he simply mentioned my being ‘a fellow teacher’ and one anxious to see the effects of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> for motives other than mere curiosity. Not a word was said—and I am sure no one could have guessed—about the objects I would wish to have described; yet they were described by Miss Brackett with a promptness, accuracy, and detail that amazed me. You must also remember that, in the course of my conversation with you, I had admitted that I was, as I truly was before this trial, a skeptic on the whole subject. I was only to be convinced by evidence that seemed irresistible to me, and I was determined to watch every circumstance, look, and movement that might pass before me with the closest scrutiny. I distinctly remember that this was also your evidently sincere and repeatedly expressed desire.

“ Meeting by chance my friend Mr. Joseph Harrington, Jr., of this place, who assured me of his strong desire to witness a display of somnambulic <term>clairvoyance</term>, if it existed, I requested the privilege of having him accompany me in your presence. Mr. Metcalf, at whose house Miss B. was then residing, very kindly and politely granted this request.

After calling on Dr. Capron, the <term>magnetizer</term>, with Mr. Harrington, I stated the motive that led me to visit him and request the favor of seeing his patient in a <term>magnetic sleep</term>. Once the hour was set, we went to Mr. Metcalf’s at 7:30 P.M. and were introduced to Miss Brackett. Dr. Capron arrived shortly after, along with several other gentlemen and ladies who were introduced one by one. In a few minutes, he proposed to begin the process of <term>magnetizing</term>. Regarding the process of <term>magnetizing</term>, I will only mention one or two phenomena that I have not seen described elsewhere. After Miss Brackett was apparently in a deep sleep, Dr. Capron asked us to observe the effect of pointing his fingers toward her hand, without touching it, from several inches away. The experiment was tried repeatedly on both the right and left hands, according to instructions, and was successful every time with the same result. No words were spoken and no signs were given that could have indicated which hand would be approached. We were then invited to try the same experiment ourselves, and we did so, but without any effect at all.

"SIR: In a conversation with you a few evenings ago, you asked me for a short sketch of what I had seen of the phenomenon called <term>somnambulism</term>.

"In reply, I can only say that my observation has been confined principally to one case, and that of a young lady of this city, known to you. I first saw her in the latter part of May, and having previously heard much but seen nothing, I was, like most others, rather skeptical regarding the facts related to me by those who had witnessed them. She was also made to see and describe distinctly the number of persons in the room, articles of small size wrapped in many thicknesses of cloth, or in the pockets

It is possible that Deleuze then had in mind the late Georget, who had published his work on physiology a few years earlier. I am sure the reader will appreciate my translation of the brief notice regarding him written by M. Foissac on page 283.

> “The experiments at the Hôtel Dieu have proved the reality of a specific agent, entirely independent of the patient’s imagination. Those at La Salpêtrière afford instances of the extraordinary phenomena of somnambulism, produced and tested by men who are a credit to science, and whose talents and integrity no one has yet dared to dispute. It was not a love for the supernatural, nor a desire for notoriety, which induced M. Georget to study the subject. In his work on madness, he inserted the following passage: ‘As long as these magnetizers conduct their experiments in secret, aided by their accomplices; as long as they do not perform their miracles before the Academy of Sciences or the Faculty of Medicine, they must allow us to skip the trouble of refuting their fantasies or their beliefs.’ But Georget’s skepticism having been shaken by the experiments at the Hôtel Dieu, he examined with caution what he at first rejected with disdain; and, six months after writing the preceding lines, he added in a note while his work was in press that he had since witnessed several magnetic phenomena. He stated that he had personally put several of his recovering patients to sleep and caused them to speak, of which we shall present a very brief analysis.

"The therapeutic resources of his <term>somnambulists</term> presented nothing very remarkable. They rarely used any but those remedies which were used daily in their presence—bloodletting, leeches, baths, <term>moxas</term>, blisters, and a few potions. He always administered everything they prescribed for themselves and never had reason to regret doing so. 'It was curious,' he says, 'to see them, when awake, protest against their own prescriptions while blisters or moxas were being prepared.' One of them, however, had eighteen or twenty moxas applied to herself, along with several <term>setons</term> (or issues) and a great number of blisters, in the space of eighteen months.

"Georget could, at will, deprive his somnambulists of sensation. Their skin was totally insensitive to the intense irritation of hot water heavily infused with ground mustard seed, and even to the burning of the moxa—a burning and irritation which were extremely painful when, by his command, the skin regained its sensibility.

Six months after writing this article, he had observed many other new and extraordinary facts. He promised, in a note, to report an instance in the chapter on epilepsy; but when he traced the history of that disease in his second volume, he added that the reason which had made him defer the publication of these phenomena to the article on <term>Magnetism</term> induced him to put it off to another period. He says, nevertheless, the person to whom he referred had displayed to him instances of foresight and clairvoyance so astonishing that he had never read anything so extraordinary in any work on Magnetism, not even in those of Petetin.

This somnambulist, Pétronille, declared that a great fright would cure her. After she had been subjected to one, she assured her friends, while in <term>somnambulism</term>, that she was radically cured. In fact, she experienced no new attack for three months, whereas before she used to have two every day.

The author of *Cures Effected in France* states, in his first volume, page 259, that this patient, Pétronille, said one day to Dr. Londe—one of the French physicians sent into Poland to observe the cholera—that in fifteen days he would have an affair of honor and would be wounded. ' In the *Physiology of the Nervous System*, Georget makes no mention of the names of his <term>somnambulists</term>, nor of the place where he conducted his experiments, nor of the numerous witnesses—physicians and others—who were convinced, like himself. *It is because,* he says, '*we live in an age when it is permitted to conceal our belief in <term>Magnetism</term>.*'

' How shall we reconcile this timidity with the courageous tribute he pays in his work to all useful discoveries, and especially to <term>Magnetism</term>? The true reason for his reserve and silence was the fear of displeasing those who managed the hospitals, who had strictly forbidden all experiments of that nature. He proposed to publish the results of his observations in more detail at a later date, if his time permitted. He expressed this desire to me during the last interview I had with him; he wished to restart his experiments and devote himself entirely to new research. "For I am persuaded," he said to me, "that great truths have escaped observers, but far from accusing them of exaggeration, I believe they have kept below reality in their accounts. I believe, for example, that there is *no perfect mode of treatment except that which <term>somnambulists</term> prescribe for themselves, and that it is possible to make their admirable instinct useful to others.* In one disease (<term>fluxion de poitrine</term> <note>inflammation of the lungs or pneumonia</note>), every physician knows that bleeding is necessary, but he does not know the precise moment for the operation, which vein should be used, and the exact quantity of blood that must be drawn, etc."'

' He then read to me the details of his first experiment at the <term>Salpêtrière</term>. The woman whom he magnetized became somnambulistic and, in the midst of great agitation, told him that at a certain period she would be attacked by a serious disease and die from it on a specific day and at a specific hour. Georget, not then knowing any works in which facts of this kind were mentioned, and unaware that <term>somnambulists</term> could themselves provide the means of preventing the effects of their predictions, believed it must necessarily happen. Full of terror and grief, he hastened to wake her; and, at the time indicated, she fell victim to the disease she had foreseen.

## FROM DR. TOOTHAKER.

### “ MR. T. C. HARTSHORN:

-> “ CAMBRIDGEPORT, December 6, 1837. <-

> “ DEAR SIR: Yours of the 2nd of this month was duly received; since then, my engagements have been such that, until the present moment, I have had no opportunity to answer it. I am perfectly willing to provide you with any facts within my knowledge on the subject of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> that are of a character suited for a popular work. The details of some cures in which I have used it successfully as a remedy would be better suited to the columns of a medical journal, where they may appear at some future time.
>
> My attention was directed particularly to the subject of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> nearly a year ago by the urgent request of a literary friend that I should read the report of the French Academy. I was, at first, entirely incredulous and unwilling even to read it attentively. But I soon found there was testimony of such a character in its favor as to demand a candid examination of the subject from every physician. To further satisfy myself of the reality of the alleged phenomena, I began experiments upon a girl, aged about sixteen, in whose case <term>idiocy</term> and <term>mania</term> were combined. I thought her a favorable subject for experiments, as there was no possibility of deception. After two or three sessions, I succeeded in producing evident drowsiness, as was apparent to all present. She gaped several times, drooled, and presented other phenomena that are common precursors to sleep. When in this state, she would always start suddenly, as if to relieve herself of its spell, and has never gone into a sound <term>magnetic sleep</term>. On one occasion, she immediately afterward left the room and went upstairs into her bedroom alone, which she had never before done in her life.

‘A year ago last <unclear>s</unclear>ummer, I was requested to magnetize Mrs. F., who, along with other ailments, had a pain between the shoulders. “About a year ago, I had occasion to magnetize Mrs. L., a French lady, who, for many years, had been afflicted with violent periodic headaches, with excessive vomiting, and some more serious ailments. The day after the first sitting, she felt much better, and she continued to improve very rapidly. However, on the morning of the sixth or seventh day of her treatment, at about 10 o’clock, her husband came to tell me that his wife had a violent headache and a very great tendency to vomit. I immediately went to see her. She was sitting by the fire, having prepared some tea to aid the tendency. I magnetized her head only, before she had taken anything. She soon felt better, and in half an hour the pain had almost subsided. I left her. In the evening, I returned and found her very well. She said she had not vomited, and, at 1 o’clock, she had dined with a very good appetite.

## FROM DR. KNOX.

“PROVIDENCE, September 24, 1837.
“Mr. T. C. HARTSHORN:
“DEAR SIR: You requested me to communicate to you some facts in <term>Animal Magnetism</term> which I had observed. Although I cannot certainly attach much importance to them, yet, if you can make any use of them, they are perfectly at your service.
“A few evenings ago, being in company where the subject of <term>Animal Magnetism</term>—at present such an engrossing theme—was the topic of conversation, I was requested to magnetize some person present for the amusement of the company. I declined this, remarking at the same time that I had frequently known peculiar sensations to be produced locally by <term>magnetic passes</term>, and offering to make the attempt. In this, much beyond my own expectation and to the amusement of the company, I was completely successful. The magnetic operations, continued for two minutes, produced complete paralysis of the left arm. Besides the complete loss of muscular power, the arm lost, to a certain degree, its sensibility, and its temperature was somewhat reduced. The firm health and previous skepticism of the subject of this experiment combined to render the result remarkable; while her unquestionable truthfulness, her eloquent look of surprise, and her repeated assertions ruled out all suspicion of deception. There were present, on this occasion, Dr. Parsons and General Greene, of Providence.
“I have frequently made the same experiment, and, in the majority of cases, some peculiar sensations have been the result; generally a sense of weight in the arm, a degree of immobility when compared with the other arm, and, though less frequently, a sense of prickling, such as occurs when the arm or foot is said to be ‘asleep.’ Whether these results are the product of an excited imagination or a direct influence of the will of the magnetizer, I shall not attempt to decide. At the same time, I must honestly admit that a skepticism, somewhat more than philosophical, with which I commenced the investigation of the claims of <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, has been overcome by facts which I have witnessed (and

# NOTE XXXIII.
## INSENSIBILITY TO PAIN.
### FROM DR. ESTEN.

> "PROVIDENCE, November 13, 1837.
> "DEAR SIR,—In the appendix of Deleuze, I find it given in the notes as an opinion that the <term>somnambulist</term> always appears to know what the <term>magnetizer</term> is doing, and therefore he cannot perform a surgical operation without producing pain. I am led by the experiments which I have tried to think this is not *always* the case. I think the patient, in the <term>somnambulic state</term>, may sometimes know what the <term>magnetizer</term> is doing, even while he is performing a surgical operation, and may assist in the operation, and still be insensible to pain. This perhaps depends very much upon the degree of sympathy which the operator has for his patient—a sympathy that induces apprehensions lest the patient should suffer under the operation.
> "On the 28th of last October, a lady, in company with a friend of hers, called on me to have some teeth filled. One, in particular, was so badly decayed, and so sensitive, that the touch of an instrument produced severe pain, so much so that she could not endure to have it filled until she was <term>magnetized</term>. Knowing that she had been frequently <term>magnetized</term>, I obtained permission to make use of it on this occasion.

Deleuze says that the influence of the <term>magnetizer</term> will be felt even in the waking state. I have evidence of a very curious nature to prove this assertion.

Everyone who takes the proper way to convince himself of the existence of the force called <term>Mesmerism</term>—that is, by attempting proofs on individuals whose state of health he desires to benefit—will find nothing more common than this influence over <term>somnambulists</term>. Georget seems not to have known this, for he might have prevented the repugnance which his patients manifested when they were treated with <term>moxas</term> <note>A moxa is a cone of combustible material burned on the skin as a medical counter-irritant.</note> and <term>blisters</term> <note>In historical medicine, a 'blister' or 'blistering agent' was a substance applied to the skin to cause a blister, intended to draw out illness.</note> of their own prescription. The reader is referred to the letter of Dr. Robbins, at the twenty-sixth note, for some curious results. In a subsequent letter, that gentleman states that he does not find the plan equally effective with everyone. A deep-seated addiction to tobacco in its various forms has been entirely destroyed, even though the patient—a young medical student of about twenty years of age—knew nothing of the cause of it while in his ordinary state. Many weeks have passed, but I am informed that the addiction has not yet returned.

The physician is someone in whom we place our trust in a special way, and therefore we are careful, first of all, to choose someone we can rely on, considering not only his skill but also certain qualities of the mind and the heart that justify our choice. If the physician we have selected suggests trying <term>Mesmerism</term> to supplement his remedies, we do not require any more trust than we already place in him, provided we have been guided by the right reasons and have not made a mistake in our selection. He is the appropriate person to use this method, as long as he is in good health and has the wisdom to conduct a trial despite his prejudices against it.

However, there are certain requirements for a <term>magnetizer</term> that are not found in some physicians. I can do no better than to recommend reading the two chapters mentioned above. The principles presented in them are supported by the facts included in this note and by the experience of many physicians with whom I have spoken. Many men of science are sincerely involved in the investigation—not, I hope, with partisan feelings, but with a genuine desire to do good. At this very time, even though the initial excitement has mostly subsided, there are more <term>somnambulists</term> and more patients under treatment than at any earlier period. Their numbers may be estimated at several hundreds in this and the neighboring States. The number of <term>somnambulists</term> mentioned in this appendix is more than sixty, not including those who are simply placed into the <term>Mesmeric state</term>, who are much more numerous.

The change was obvious to others as well as myself in the immediate and almost entire restoration of my voice. In the morning, the <term>Mesmeric</term> influence seemed to have worn off, and my illness resumed its course, but it was so much improved that I did not think it necessary to trouble my friend for another application of the remedy. If I might be allowed to use such an expression, I would say that it was three-quarters cured.
