"*Case sixth.*—In March, 1842, I attended Miss —— for a spinal condition. It was extremely tender—very slight pressure produced intense pain on the spot, and in distant parts of the system connected by nervous communication with the parts of the spine being pressed, as well as faintness. By passing my hand over the spine for a few minutes, the tenderness was entirely removed, so that any degree of pressure could be endured without discomfort. I then proceeded to make two long and deep issues <note>An "issue" was a surgically created sore or incision kept open to allow for the drainage of fluids, believed to have therapeutic benefits.</note> with caustic potash, one on each side of the spine. During the whole operation, she declared that she did not suffer the slightest pain, but felt the same sensation of pleasure which she experienced from the movement of my hand while Mesmerizing. Just at the close of the operation, she complained of nausea, an effect which I have often witnessed when Mesmerizing the back, unless some passes are made at the same time over the stomach. The most severe pain from these issues was subsequently removed at any time in a few moments by someone passing their hand over them.

"*Case seventh.*—In February, 1842, I visited Miss —— under the following circumstances. She had recently been treated by a quack, who had followed a stimulating treatment. This had brought on acute inflammation of the mucous membrane of the stomach and bowels, accompanied by uncontrollable vomiting and diarrhea. The pain was constant and terribly severe. Other symptoms were alarming. Her face was pale and sunken, and covered with a clammy sweat—her pulse was a weak and almost indistinguishable flutter.

### FROM DR. CLEVELAND.

> “ PROVIDENCE, August 4, 1843.
> 
> “ DEAR SIR,—In compliance with your request, I have made several experiments upon the memory, or rather upon the power of recalling events, which have proved very satisfactory.
> 
> “ The first experiment consisted in inducing the mind to recall, or to be impressed with, all or any of the past events of life, back to the earliest period possible. Many incidents of maturer years, which had long been forgotten, were mentioned with a perfect remembrance of their occurrence—not, however, by the ordinary means of the accidental association of ideas, but, as it were, by a sudden impression. The events of earlier life, without that clearness of memory as to their certainty, were very distinctly and minutely recalled and described, as were those that occurred at a period of life so early as to not be substantiated by the evidence of memory, but appearing like dreams. Events that took place before the <term>magnetized</term> person was ten months old were by her perfectly and very minutely described, although she had to depend upon the testimony of others as to their reality. Individuals were described and called by name whom she had not seen, or whose names she had not heard mentioned, since she was two years old—more than twenty years ago. The events of infancy and early childhood appeared more to her like a dream than a reality. The restraints under which she was placed when she became able to crawl about the house—the circumstance of falling downstairs and the person who picked her up—her first attempts to walk—her peculiar favorites, etc., etc.—all of which occurred before she was eleven months old, were described with much feeling and accuracy, as tested by the recollection of others in the family, who were surprised at her mentioning them without knowing the reason for her doing so.
> 
> “ These exercises were continued for two days. The mind was then directed to the recalling of particular events. I say *directed*, for in these experiments my subject was not consulted. The influence was exerted while she was in a <term>magnetic state</term>, and arrangements were made the day previous to their going into action.

### NOTE XXXVII.

NEUROLOGY.—The following letter from Dr. Buchanan will be read with interest by all who have had an opportunity to witness his experiments. His classes in New York, Boston, and other places have been formed among men of science and literature, and composed chiefly of such individuals, including many physicians; and they have, in several published reports, expressed a very favorable opinion both of Dr. Buchanan as a man and of his system, as demonstrable by experiments. Some accounts of these experiments, which are performed on persons in their natural state, have been given in periodicals; but the public will soon have Dr. Buchanan’s exposition of his own system. Dr. Buchanan possesses learning and science, and the talent of applying them. His error, if he has fallen into one, may consist in supposing the absence of the *vis voluntatis* <note>the power of the will</note> in his experiments; for he says that some of these effects can be produced by the will alone. But whatever fate may befall his theory, his facts are very novel in character and easy to be tested; they cannot fail to attract the attention of philosophical minds.

“ PROVIDENCE, April 12, 1843.

“ SIR: The sketch of the principles of <term>Neurology</term> which you desire may be given in a few words, despite the complexity and scale of the science. It would require a library to give us a complete and accurate understanding of the subject, although the core principles of the science may be stated on a single page.

“ The science of Neurology is the whole science of man. It explains the functions of the brain and proves that through these functions we may learn all his mental powers and all the laws of his <term>physiology</term>. It proves that the mind of man is a <term>microcosm</term>, in which we may discover indications of the laws and facts of external nature.

“ This science owes its origin to the discovery which I first publicly announced in the month of April, 1841: that the human brain could be excited and compelled to manifest the functions of its different convolutions. By pursuing this discovery and exciting each convolution so as to make its functions predominate over all others (as, for instance, by exciting <term>Alimentiveness</term> until hunger became uncontrollable), I have succeeded in demonstrating the mental functions of the different organs—which in most respects are in harmony with the theory of <term>Gall</term> and <term>Spurzheim</term>—and in establishing the controlling power of the brain over the physiological phenomena of the body.

“ A complex system of <term>Phrenology</term> and Physiology has been developed by my experiments, which might very properly be called <term>Anthropology</term>. But as this system has been developed by experiments upon the brain, and as the nervous substance of the body is the seat of its vital powers, that science which explains the human vital functions is merely the science of the nervous substance, and should therefore be called Neurology.

“ By the term nervous substance, I refer specifically to the <term>encephalon</term>, which is the most important mass of nervous substance in the body. The study of its functions gives us the whole science of man. The mind holds its communication with the physical world through the brain, which forms its connecting link with the body, and which transmits its volitions and its continual influence to the body. A paper, for instance, was placed in her hand (it being at the same time held by Dr. Buchanan), which speedily produced such a powerful narcotic effect as to create some alarm: and it was several minutes before she could be recovered by Dr. Buchanan from its poisonous influence. As she was being restored to a state of consciousness, she made several efforts to vomit, but after the passage of eight or ten minutes, during which time various passes <note>gestures or hand movements used in mesmerism to direct "fluid"</note> were made for her relief, she seemed quite recovered.
On examination, the paper was found to contain the extract of stramonium (Jamestown weed <note>also known as Jimson weed</note>.) One of the papers which had been previously tried, and found to produce an "irritating effect and copper-like taste in the mouth," and which had been laid aside for subsequent trial, was now again presented.
The effect, as it now perhaps proved less irritating, she described as "stimulating, heating, and exciting," to a greater degree than she could well bear. This was opened and found to contain Cayenne pepper. Another paper was presented which induced narcotic and sickening effects somewhat similar to those of the stramonium. It was immediately removed, and the paper, on being opened, was found to contain opium.

It ought to be observed here that Dr. Buchanan’s experiments detailed above were made upon an impressible person in the natural state; and are therefore conclusive. He calls the agent by which one individual makes a physiological impression upon another, when in contact, *Neuraura*, an appropriate name until it shall be identified with the universal fluid of *La Place*. This fluid, says Dr. Buchanan, is radiated and conducted freely from the human hand.

It should be remembered that Mesmer maintained the existence of such a fluid, and perhaps justice as well as convenience would suggest the propriety of continuing to call it the Mesmeric fluid: in the same manner as we call the one

We are so far from being acquainted with all the agencies of nature, and with their different modes of action, that it would be unphilosophical to deny their existence, because in the present state of our knowledge they are unexplainable to us.”—*La Place*, *Traité Analytique du Calcul des Probabilités*, p. 41.

### NOTE XLII.—Page 324.

*Magnetism a Science.*—As objections are sometimes made to the word "science" as applied to Mesmerism, I have avoided the use of it in the appendix; but as some of my correspondents have used it, and as Deleuze himself does not hesitate to do so, it may be expedient to consider whether it is entitled to that name.

We apply the term to any subject of study that has certain fixed principles, such as music, electricity, or Galvanism. The whole science of electricity, so far as it is known according to the Franklinian theory, is based upon two principles.

But there are many facts not reducible to these two principles; perhaps they refer to laws not yet discovered. Its relation to terrestrial Magnetism and to Galvanism is not ascertained: theory supposes them to be modifications of the same agent. If it were necessary for all the principles to be de-

<header>NEW APPENDIX.</header>

veloped, before a subject is honored with the name of science, we may have been too hasty regarding electricity. And if we were to examine the claims of all the other branches of human knowledge to this term, we should find them, by the same argument, equally unfounded; for every one of them may have unexplored or undiscovered laws. Properly speaking, we would not have a single science.

Again, if we limit the application to those subjects which have a certain number of discovered laws, how shall we determine the number that is necessary? If more than two are required, then electricity is no science.

Everyone who reads the *Practical Instruction* will observe that Mesmerism has two fundamental principles, which are to be regarded in its application.

First, this agent must be employed *with attention*.

Secondly, it must be employed with the *proper intention*.

If anyone objects that these principles refer solely to the conditions of its action, it is easy to say the same thing of the two laws of electricity, which do not claim to explain the agent itself.

The laws of both of these agents are easily demonstrated. Further, there are certain circumstances which are requisite before the demonstration can be made. It cannot, therefore, be argued with propriety that Mesmerism is improperly termed a science simply because its effects are not always producible; nor can it be argued from the consideration that we do not perfectly know the circumstances which impede its action. Electricity would still be a science, even if we were ignorant of the disturbing cause arising from the moisture of the atmosphere.

Neither can the existence or the non-existence of a fluid determine this question, or affect it in the least. Electricity cannot be proved to be a fluid. The light which we see when we apply the discharger to a Leyden jar may be nothing more than the sudden and violent compression of the atmosphere, which attends the restoration of the equilibrium. If there is a fluid, it is invisible; otherwise, we should see it in the Leyden jar when fully charged.

To show the favor with which this work was received when the first edition was published, we append a few notices from the press:

### (Extracts from Providence Papers, noticing the First Edition.)

Mr. Thomas C. Hartshorn, of this city, has published Part I of the work of J. P. F. Deleuze, with the title of “Practical Instruction in Animal Magnetism.” We have always been skeptical about this subject, probably because we have taken no pains to obtain evidence of its truth; and we have probably been prevented from seeking this evidence, first, because we did not wish to be carried away by a momentary excitement; and second, because, as we frankly confess, we have no desire to be convinced of its truth until satisfied that, if true, it will be productive of more good than evil—and we do not believe that it will be.

But as for the work before us, though other pressing occupations have prevented us from giving it a thorough reading, there are two things for which we can vouch. Whatever Mr. H. does is well done; and, therefore, the public may have the utmost confidence in his translation as being a faithful and elegant one; and be assured that his own notes are written with the highest degree of candor and good feeling. — *Republican Herald.*

Fully aware of the ridicule to which the devotees of Mesmerism have been subjected, he shows no disposition to shun the criticisms of those who have endeavored, from the very beginning, to overthrow the labors of those who are toiling in this new field of philosophy.
